The Complainant alleges that Ali Benidir was arrested on 29 August 1996 by "Patriots" and has not been seen again by his family. Neither his arrest nor his detention were legally motivated and recorded in any official register. The Complainant maintains that the investigations lacked the effective and efficient character required in these circumstances, and the official authorities persist in concealing the fate that was reserved for him. For the Complainant, this arrest and the secrecy surrounding his detention constitute arbitrary detention under Article 6 of the African Charter.

The Complainant refers to the Commission's jurisprudence which considers that the enforced disappearance of a person is a violation of Article 6 as well as the jurisprudence of the United Nations Human Rights Committee which also considers that the incommunicado detention of a person constitutes a violation of Article 9 of the Covenant which enshrines the right to liberty and security of person.

The Complainant alleges that the right to a judicial remedy was violated not only with regard to Ali Benidir but also with regard to his mother Houria Berkane, wife of Benidir. He maintains that the Benidir family approached all the competent authorities of the Algerian State and exhausted all local remedies both before the judicial and administrative authorities. The Complainant further maintains that all the steps proved useless insofar as they yielded no result.

The Complainant further alleges that following the promulgation of Ordinance No. 06-01, any denunciation or complaint by the Benidir family will be declared inadmissible. He indicates that Article 45 of Ordinance No. 06-01 prohibits recourse to justice to shed light on the most serious crimes such as enforced disappearances, requiring the competent judicial authorities to declare any denunciation or complaint inadmissible.

The Complainant affirms that the entry into force of Ordinance No. 06-01 prevents any judicial action against State agents. Indeed, under Article 45 of this ordinance: "No proceedings may be brought, individually or collectively against members of any component of the defence and security forces of the Republic [...]". He continues that Article 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01 goes further in that it provides for a prison sentence of three to five years and a fine of 250,000 DA to 500,000 DA for: "anyone who, by his statements, writings or any other act, uses or instrumentalises the wounds of the national tragedy, to undermine the institutions of the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria, weaken the State, harm the honourability of its agents who have served it with dignity, or tarnish the image of Algeria internationally. Criminal proceedings are initiated ex officio by the public prosecutor's office. In the event of a repeat offence, the penalty provided for in this article is doubled".

According to the Complainant, all the steps undertaken by the parents of Ali Benidir after the entry into force of Ordinance No. 06-01 remained in vain. Indeed, the attorney general of the Hussein Dey court issued an order of non-suit on 18 April 2006. According to the Complainant, Ordinance No. 06-01 is merely a legal consecration of an already widespread practice in that the Algerian authorities refuse to shed light on the fate of the disappeared and conduct no impartial and thorough investigation.

The Complainant reports that Article 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01 provides for imprisonment and a fine for anyone who "uses or instrumentalises the wounds of the national tragedy, to undermine the institutions of the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria, weaken the State, harm the honourability of its agents who have served it with dignity, or tarnish the image of Algeria internationally".

He indicates that by virtue of this article, the family is prevented from communicating about their grief and distress caused by the disappearance of their son. Thus, Houria Berkane, wife of Benidir, risks imprisonment of three to five years and a fine of 250,000 DA to 500,000 DA each time she speaks of her distress or mobilises in a peaceful gathering in favour of truth and justice. This constitutes a direct violation of the freedom of expression provided for in Article 9 of the African Charter.

The Complainant further cites the concluding observations of the United Nations Human Rights Committee in the context of the examination of Algeria's report in 2007, which recommends that the State party "repeal any provision of Ordinance No. 06/01 implementing the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation, [...] which undermines freedom of expression as well as the right of every person to have access to an effective remedy against human rights violations, both at the national and international level".

In addition to the violation of the rights guaranteed in Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) and 9(2) of the Charter, the Complainant alleges the violation of Article 2 § 3 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and Articles 13, 14 and 19 of the Declaration of 18 December 1992 on the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance.

In its brief on the merits, the Respondent State once again raises the objection relating to the inadmissibility of the case for three reasons. Firstly, it maintains that the Complainant did not exhaust local remedies and explains that the alleged facts were brought to the attention of the Algerian justice system by the father of the victim, Mr Mahmoud Benidir, who filed a complaint for abduction before the Hussein Dey court.

The Respondent State puts forward that all the investigations undertaken did not convince the examining magistrate as to the merit of the accusations; which led the magistrate to issue an order of non-suit which, appealed by the complainant, was confirmed by the Indictment Chamber of the Court of Algiers for absence of sufficient elements in the procedural file making it possible to engage the responsibility of the persons suspected by the civil party.

The Respondent State maintains that local remedies were not exhausted because the civil party did not use another remedy offered by law, namely, the appeal in cassation before the Supreme Court. The Respondent State considers the attitude of renouncing the use of a remedy offered by law as an acceptance of the court's decision.

The Respondent State concludes that the remedies recognised by law not having been exhausted in their entirety, the complainant cannot bring the complaint before the Commission, on pain of violating the principle by virtue of which an international mechanism cannot rule on a case which has not been brought before the national courts and for which all remedies have not been exhausted.

Secondly, the Respondent State puts forward the lis pendens of the Benidir Ali case before the Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances (WGEID). It affirms that the WGEID of the United Nations Human Rights Council remains seized of the Benidir Ali case, which is part of the allegations of disappearances that occurred in Algeria, appearing in the list in the WGEID's annual report, under No. 3402.

For the Respondent State, the allegations of disappearances are examined within the framework of the WGEID's procedures for a reconciliation of the official lists of victims of the national tragedy, presented by the Algerian Government, which were the subject of a settlement under the provisions of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation. The Benidir case is listed under No. 263, entered as "disappeared, declared deceased by the rightful claimants who have been compensated".

The Respondent State affirms that exchanges of correspondence, contacts and formal meetings continue between the representatives of the Algerian Government and the members of the WGEID, on the basis of the working rules and procedures of this body, with a view to reaching either decisions of closure or clarification of the cases submitted.

Thirdly, the Respondent State challenges the mandate of Ms Yous Nassera to act on behalf of the rightful claimants. The Respondent State considers that Ms Yous Nassera, acting on behalf of the association "Collective of Families of the Disappeared in Algeria", an NGO under French law based in Paris, cannot claim to legally represent the members of a family which has benefited from the mechanism for the care of the families of victims put in place in application of the provisions of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation.

The Respondent State attests that the rightful claimants of the disappeared Benidir Ali, declared deceased, a victim of the national tragedy, have benefited since February 2007 from compensation in the form of a monthly pension distributed between the mother Berkane Houria, the widow Boudahane Nadjat and the daughter Benidir Anfal; the father, Benidir Mahmoud, having died in 2008. It further maintains that the rightful claimants of Benidir Ali (his mother, his wife and his daughter) voluntarily adhered to the care provided for by the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation, within the framework of the political settlement of the national tragedy, adopted by referendum.

Therefore, the Respondent State considers that neither Ms Yous Nassera, nor the Collective of Families of the Disappeared, can rely on any duly established mandate of representation to act or to submit in the name and on behalf of the rightful claimants of Benidir Ali a communication before the African Commission or any other body. For all these reasons, the Respondent State requests the Commission to review its decision and to declare the present Communication inadmissible.

Regarding the arguments on the merits of the Communication, the main ground invoked by the Respondent State is that the Complainant's allegations are unfounded because the Algerian justice system did its duty properly. The Respondent State maintains that the examining magistrate and the Indictment Chamber conducted their investigations and worked on all leads, in accordance with their respective mandates, in strict compliance with national criminal procedures, to help bring out the truth. The State considers that it has discharged all the duties that were required in such circumstances.

Concerning Ordinance No. 06-01, the Respondent State maintains that the Complainant's invocation of this document is unfounded insofar as the court's decision was based on facts, hearings of the persons implicated and of witnesses, confrontations and other means of investigation aimed at shedding light on this disappearance. According to the Respondent State, the said Ordinance never served as a basis for the decisions of the two investigating courts in the handling of the Benidir case.

The Respondent State explains that the Complainant cannot invoke the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation and its implementing texts to exempt himself from not having initiated the available judicial proceedings, constituting local remedies, inciting the Commission to share his suspicion and his preconceptions about the foundations of Algerian justice and the independence of the Judge.

The Respondent State considers the complainant's argument as eminently subjective and politically motivated, and this in his systematic approach of calling into question Algerian justice and the option of reconciliation adopted by the Algerian people in its immense majority.

The Respondent State therefore requests the Commission to find that: the present case was the subject of judicial treatment, in accordance with the procedures in force; the court based itself on facts that were brought to its knowledge and on the judicial investigation that followed to form a conviction and render its decisions; Ordinance No. 06-01 was never invoked by the court; the Algerian State has committed none of the alleged violations.

In response to the Respondent State's observations on the admissibility of the communication, the Complainant takes note of the observations of the Algerian State. He wishes, however, to emphasise that the Respondent State's observations are identical to those already raised at the admissibility stage of the Communication in its earlier briefs and in view of which the Commission has already ruled on the admissibility of the communication. The Complainant deplores that despite the Commission's decision on admissibility, the Respondent State continues to contest the said decision, endlessly delaying the examination of the communication on the merits. He therefore requests the Commission to disregard the State's arguments; to reject its request for inadmissibility and to rule on the merits of the Benidir communication.

In response to the Respondent State's observations on the merits, the Complainant refutes the Respondent State's assertions according to which investigations were conducted by the examining magistrate or the indictment chamber to help bring out the truth about the disappearance of Ali Benidir. The Complainant reiterates that at the end of more than ten years of proceedings, the various complaints of Mr and Mrs Benidir to the different authorities led only to non-suits, referrals, or dismissals without further action, thus calling into question the seriousness of the various investigations conducted in this case. The fate of Ali Benidir has thus still not been clarified. As for the patriots who were formally named by two eyewitnesses as being the perpetrators of the arrest of Benidir which was followed by his enforced disappearance, they were never troubled by Algerian justice for these facts.

Furthermore, the Complainant indicates that Ali Benidir's mother is in no way driven by political motivations and is in no way engaging in "a flagrant abusive misuse of procedure", but simply wishes to find her son. On the contrary, she seized the Algerian courts with her late husband so that an effective and impartial investigation would be conducted and prosecutions brought against those responsible. Ali Benidir's parents therefore cooperated fully with the Algerian authorities and Mrs Houria Berkane wishes more than anything that the Algerian authorities do everything that is legally possible to discover the truth about the fate of her son.

The Complainant also refutes the Respondent State's argument according to which the Algerian judicial authorities never invoked Ordinance No. 06-01. Indeed, the CFDA wishes to recall that Mahmoud Benidir was summoned on 13 March 2007 by the deputy attorney general of the Hussein Dey Court. In the minutes of this summons, the latter explicitly requests the father: "to apply the procedure cited by Ordinance No. 06-01". On the objection of inadmissibility for non-exhaustion of local remedies, lis pendens and the standing of the Complainant to act on behalf of the victims.

On the objection raised by the Respondent State concerning the inadmissibility of the Communication, the Commission considers that there is no need to resume the analysis on admissibility insofar as it has already declared the Communication admissible and rejected the motion for review. These two decisions are therefore authoritative and form the procedural basis of the proceedings on the merits in the context of which the Respondent State has submitted its conclusions.

As for the examination on the merits, the Commission will determine on the basis of the facts and arguments submitted by the parties whether Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) and 9(2) of the African Charter have been violated.

On these grounds, the Commission refers to its jurisprudence in Working Group on Strategic Litigation v. Democratic Republic of Congo to recall that its mandate specifically covers the rights contained in the Charter. By virtue of the provisions of Article 60 of the Charter, the Commission may however draw inspiration from principles included in other human rights conventions without however extending the scope of its material jurisdiction to the said instruments. Where appropriate, a link must be established between these principles and those contained in the Charter.

In the present case, the Commission notes that the Complainant does not demonstrate such a link. Moreover, considering that the rights protected by the provisions of the said instruments are usefully guaranteed by the Charter, there is no need to draw inspiration from them.

In sum, regarding the allegations of violation of instruments other than the Charter, the Commission decides, in view of the foregoing, to set them aside from the examination on the merits. The said examination will, consequently, be limited to the allegations of violation of the provisions of Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) and 9(2) of the Charter.

Under Article 1 of the African Charter, States parties recognise the rights, duties and freedoms enshrined in this charter and undertake to adopt legislative or other measures to give effect to them. A State's failure to perform its obligation under Article 1 of the Charter may open the way to the violation of substantive rights or at least limit their enjoyment. In this regard, the Commission refers to its jurisprudence to note that, in principle, non-observance of the obligation prescribed in Article 1 is constituted once a violation of a provision of the Charter is found. It follows that any allegation of violation of Article 1 of the African Charter must be supported by proof of the disregard of another substantive right guaranteed by the Charter. The Commission will therefore examine, prior to the determination of a possible violation of Article 1, the allegations of violation of the substantive rights guaranteed by Articles 4, 5, 6, 7(1) and 9(2) of the African Charter.

Article 4 of the African Charter provides that "Human beings are inviolable. Every human being shall be entitled to respect for his life and the integrity of his person. No one may be arbitrarily deprived of this right". Under the violations of the right to life thus guaranteed by the African Charter, the Complainant cites the enforced disappearance of Mr Benidir Ali since his arrest of 29 August 1996.

The terms "enforced disappearances" not being defined by the African Charter, the analysis will be conducted in light of other international rules in accordance with Article 61 of the African Charter in order to determine the definition. The most specific instrument in the matter is the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance of 20 December 2006.

Under the provisions of Article 2 of the said Convention, "enforced disappearance" is considered to be the arrest, detention, abduction or any other form of deprivation of liberty by agents of the State or by persons or groups of persons acting with the authorization, support or acquiescence of the State, followed by a refusal to acknowledge the deprivation of liberty or by concealment of the fate or whereabouts of the disappeared person, which place such a person outside the protection of the law.

The Commission notes that Mr Ali Benidir disappeared after his arrest on 29 August 1996 by Lahcene Aliche, Mohamed Mayouf, Mustapha Koumina, Nacer Meslem, Makhlouf Barkat and Samir Dandani, all members of the pro-government militia of the Aïn Naadja neighbourhood known by the nickname of "patriots". That the patriots carried out abductions or rackets, and that anyone refusing to collaborate with them became an enemy, an Islamist and therefore a terrorist. It also notes that at the end of more than seventeen years of proceedings, the fate of Ali BENIDIR has still not been clarified and that he allegedly lost his life in incommunicado detention. The Respondent State provides no denial of the facts as reported by the Complainant.

The Commission further notes that after the arrest of Benidir by the patriots, he was taken directly to the car park of the Aïn Naadja Town Hall as maintained by the Complainant. The Commission thus considers that the constituent element of the beginning of the enforced disappearance, namely the deprivation of liberty, is present in the present case. Moreover, from what the evidence establishes, Benidir's relatives have always insistently sought to know the truth about what happened to him, without ever obtaining an answer. The Commission deduces that the arrest, the ignorance of the place of detention and the lack of information on the fate and situation of the victim are constituent elements of an enforced disappearance with regard to Benidir.

The question that arises is whether the enforced disappearance of Benidir must be attributed to the Respondent State as maintained by the Complainant. The Commission notes that the patriots operated if not with the authorisation at least with the consent of the Respondent State. This is notably attested by the fact that the patriots carried out arrests in broad daylight without being troubled. What is more, they had barracks and a headquarters in a car park of the Aïn Naadja Town Hall. This use of a public place - the car park of a town hall - by the patriots to coordinate their activities without being troubled by the authorities is proof of the authorisation or even the acquiescence of the Respondent State to use these public places and to exercise police functions in the Aïn Naadja neighbourhood.

On the basis of this acquiescence, the arrest of Mr Ali Benidir, his detention in an unknown place and his enforced disappearance are attributable to the Respondent State. Even supposing that the patriots escaped the control of State authority, the State's responsibility would remain engaged nonetheless. This is so because Article 1 of the Charter requires States parties to adopt all appropriate measures to ensure the effective protection of the rights of all individuals within their territory and subject to their sovereignty. The undertaking of States parties to give effect to the rights guaranteed by the Charter includes not only that of respecting them, by not themselves infringing them, but also that of protecting them, which includes protection against any infringement to which they might be subject at the hands of non-State actors.

The Commission refers to its decision in Communication 389/12 - Geneviève Mbiankeu v. Cameroon in which it concluded that under Article 1 of the Charter, States are bound not only by the obligation to respect the rights of their citizens but also to protect them against violation by third parties. In accordance with the Commission's jurisprudence, if a State neglects to ensure respect for the rights contained in the African Charter, this constitutes a violation of the said Charter, even when that State or its agents are not the direct perpetrators of this violation. The Commission has also considered that human rights standards do not only contain limits on State power or on State organs. They also impose positive obligations on States to prevent and punish human rights violations committed by private actors. Indeed, human rights oblige States to protect citizens or persons within their jurisdiction against the harmful acts of third parties. Thus, an act perpetrated by a private person, and therefore not directly attributable to a State, may give rise to the responsibility of the State, not because of the act itself, but because of the lack of due diligence to prevent the violation or the failure to take the necessary measures to grant reparation to the victims.

The African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Court) reached the same conclusion in its decision in the case African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights v. Libya (Saif Al Islam Kadhafi Case). In the opinion of the African Court, the State is responsible for its actions as much as for its omissions and indeed has the obligation to adopt measures to ensure, on its territory, the application of the rights guaranteed under the African Charter. Likewise, the European Court of Human Rights ruled more extensively on the question of the positive obligation, concluding in the case Osmanoglu v. Turkey that the State must not only refrain from intentionally and unlawfully causing death, but also has the obligation to take the necessary measures to protect the life of persons within its jurisdiction. In the Case Kaya v. Turkey, the Court concluded that if the evidence was not sufficient to conclude beyond reasonable doubt that Dr Kaya had been killed by State agents, it nevertheless considered that the Turkish authorities had failed in their obligation to take reasonable measures to protect him against a real risk to his life.

The Commission notes that in the present case, Mr Benidir was allegedly arrested by the Patriots who exercised the role of police in public places without being troubled and that the State did nothing to prevent and stop the violation. It therefore concludes that the Respondent State is responsible for the disappearance of Mr Benidir.

Having concluded that the Respondent State is responsible for Benidir's disappearance, the Commission will then determine whether a disappearance can be considered an infringement of the right to life as alleged by the Complainant. To answer this question, the Commission will refer to the jurisprudence of other international courts, notably the Inter-American Court of Human Rights (the Inter-American Court) which has affirmed that the practice of enforced disappearances frequently involves the secret execution of detainees without any other form of trial, followed by the concealment of the corpse with the aim of erasing all material trace of the crime and of granting impunity to the perpetrators, which is a brutal violation of the right to life.

According to the European Court of Human Rights, the violation of the right to life in the case of a disappearance does not stop at finding the absence of material proof of the death of the person reported missing. Proof of the violation of the right to life stems not from the factual elements of an isolated case, but from relating the facts of the case to the existence or not of an official practice of enforced disappearances.

The Commission recalls to that effect the general situation that prevailed in Algeria in the 1990s, defined as the period of the "national tragedy". It therefore cannot in any way be excluded that the arrest of Benidir by the patriots for his real or supposed membership of the Islamist movement and his disappearance were such as to endanger his life.

The Commission further considers that the passage of time may have a certain bearing on the weight to be given to other indications before it can be concluded that the disappeared person may be presumed dead. It must be accepted that the more time passes without any news of the detained person, the more likely it is that he is dead. In this regard, the length of time elapsed since the arrest of Benidir is a factor to be taken into account. The Commission notes that more than 20 years have elapsed without it being possible to obtain information on the fate of Benidir Ali.

Moreover, the Commission, basing itself on the Respondent State's submissions, including notably a fact sheet drawn up by the services of the Ministry of the Interior and Local Authorities which acknowledges that the disappeared person was declared deceased, a victim of the national tragedy, accepts that Benidir is no longer of this world.

In these circumstances, the Commission is of the view that the Respondent State failed in its obligation to protect Mr Benidir Ali against enforced disappearance followed by the loss of his life and is consequently responsible for the violation of Article 4 of the African Charter.

Article 5 of the Charter provides that "Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited".

The Commission notes that the Complainant alleges that the Respondent State failed in its obligation to protect Ali Benidir against physical torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment as well as his family against moral torture following the disappearance of their relative. On this precise point, the Respondent State, in its arguments, did not provide proof of the diligence undertaken to protect the victim.
The Commission notes that the present Communication raises questions relating to torture, to the recognition of legal status and to cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment.

In its jurisprudence on torture and inhuman treatment, the Commission adopts the definition of the United Nations Committee against Torture which observes that the distinction between inhuman treatment and torture is to be sought in the nature, purpose and severity of the treatment inflicted. With particular regard to torture, the Committee emphasises, in its General Comment No. 20, that the acts in question must cause excruciating suffering intentionally inflicted, have the purpose of obtaining information or confessions, of punishing the victim for real or supposed acts and be attributable to a State agent or a person acting in that capacity. The Commission adopts this nomenclature in its decision Sudan Human Rights Organisation and Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) v. Sudan.

The Commission notes that according to the facts not contested by the Respondent State, while he was detained at the Aïn Naadja gendarmerie following his first arrest in April 1995, Mr Benidir was subjected notably to the rag torture, beating with truncheons, his genitals tied with a wire to prevent him from urinating, detention in a cell devoid of everything, flooded with water, where he had to sleep on the bare floor, naked and without a blanket.

The Commission considers that the absence of denial by the Respondent State of the facts as reported by the Complainant amounts to acquiescence, the proceedings having been adversarial. This position is consistent with the Commission's constant jurisprudence according to which "where allegations of human rights abuse go uncontested by the Respondent State, ... the Commission must decide on the facts provided by the Complainant and treat those facts as given...".

The Commission notes that these acts caused serious physical and mental suffering to the victim. It finds that these acts were intentionally inflicted by public officials (soldiers of the Aïn Naadja gendarmerie) to punish the victim and obtain information about his supposed or real links with the FIS. In these circumstances, the Commission concludes that acts of torture were committed on the person of Benidir.

Regarding the other alleged violations of Article 5, the Complainant reports acts of torture suffered by Benidir during his second arrest by the patriots in August 1996, notably arbitrary arrest, incommunicado detention without allowing him any contact with his family as well as the enforced disappearance that followed.

The Commission recalls that to be characterised as torture, the acts perpetrated must not only be severe pain or suffering, but above all caused by or at the instigation of a public authority, with the purpose of punishing or of obtaining information or a confession; the said pain or suffering being able to be physical or mental. The notable difference between torture and treatment liable to be assimilated to it is therefore to be sought in the capacity of the perpetrators.

In the present case, the perpetrators were private persons acting in public places and under the authorisation of public authority but without the official capacity of public officials. The Commission considers that even if the Victim suffered acts of a certain severity which caused him both physical and mental suffering, the perpetrators were private persons, "the patriots". Given the official capacity of the perpetrators as a necessary condition for the characterisation of certain acts as amounting to torture, in the present case, there is no need to conclude that there was torture but rather cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment.

On the allegation of the violation of the right to respect for human dignity and of the right to recognition of legal status, in its relevant jurisprudence, the Commission has established a connection of principle between torture, inhuman and degrading treatment and human dignity. This is so, among others, in the cases Modise v. Botswana and Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and Interights v. Egypt where the Commission considers that inhuman and degrading treatment necessarily violates human dignity.

The Commission has also concluded that all enforced disappearances violate a wide range of human rights, notably the right to security and dignity of the person, the right not to be subjected to torture or to any other cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment, the right to humane conditions of detention, the right to a legal personality, the right to a fair trial, the right to family life and, when the disappeared person has been killed, the right to life.

This position is consistent with the relevant international jurisprudence which considers that the enforced disappearance of persons constitutes a multiple violation which begins with a deprivation of liberty. The Inter-American Court concluded that enforced disappearance also entails an infringement of the right to recognition of legal personality enshrined in Article 3 of the American Convention, given that the disappearance of a person seeks not only to employ one of the most serious forms of removal of a person from any legal order, but also to deny his existence and to leave him in a situation of legal uncertainty before society and the State.

In all logic, enforced disappearance also violates human dignity and the recognition of legal status. It is therefore appropriate to conclude that these rights have been violated with regard to Ali Benidir.

Regarding the violation of Article 5 of the Charter with respect to Benidir's close relatives, the Complainant alleges that Ali Benidir's wife (Boudahane Nadjat), his mother and his daughter also suffered moral torture in that the disappearance of Mr Benidir, since his arrest on 29 August 1996 by the patriots, has caused anguish and distress among his relatives.

The Commission has already recognised that detaining persons without allowing them any contact with their families and refusing to inform the families of the fact and place of detention of these persons constitute inhuman treatment both for the detainee and for his family. The Commission has also established that any act leading to enforced disappearance causes suffering to the victim himself and to his family.

This position is also corroborated by international jurisprudence. In the case Maria del Calmen de Quinteros et al v. Uruguay, the Human Rights Committee established that the anguish and stress caused to a mother by the disappearance of her daughter in conditions where her fate remained unknown constitute a violation of Article 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. For its part, the Inter-American Court concluded that an enforced disappearance constitutes cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment of the victim's family in the same way as of the victim himself. It also recognised that the anguish, suffering, frustration and helplessness of a relative of the victim vis-à-vis the authorities constitute cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment. In the present case, the Commission notes the anguish and distress that the detention and disappearance of Benidir Ali caused to his relatives.

In light of the foregoing, it is appropriate to conclude that the Respondent State violated Article 5 of the Charter, notably the right not to be subjected to torture and to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment with regard to Mr Benidir as well as with regard to his mother and his relatives.

Under Article 6 of the African Charter "Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained". The Commission recalled the importance of these provisions in the Guidelines on the Conditions of Arrest, Police Custody and Pre-Trial Detention in Africa which prescribe that no one must be deprived of his liberty except on the grounds and according to the procedures laid down by law.

The Commission notes the Complainant's allegation according to which Mr Benidir was subjected to an arrest resembling an abduction for the first time and then a second time in a secret place for his supposed links with the FIS, which constitutes arbitrary detention. It is for the Commission to determine whether the victim's detention is arbitrary.

The Commission has observed that not all actions limiting the physical liberty of an individual constitute a deprivation of liberty under Article 6 of the Charter. But a deprivation of liberty that does not fall within the strict limits of the law or is for unacceptable or simply arbitrary reasons constitutes a violation of Article 6 of the Charter.
In Liesbeth Zegveld and Mussie Ephrem v. Eritrea, the Commission adopted the position that incommunicado detention constitutes a serious violation of human rights under Article 6 of the Charter.

From the Complainant's submissions, the Commission notes that Ali Benidir's first arrest was carried out in a brutal manner. Nothing reveals that his captors informed him of the reason for his arrest, let alone showed him a legal title justifying his arrest. The subsequent detention in a secret place and without contact with his family is testimony that the deprivation of liberty was carried out in violation of Article 6 of the African Charter.
The Commission considers that Benidir's detention is arbitrary. It is consequently appropriate to conclude that the provisions of Article 6 of the Charter have been violated.

Article 7(1) of the African Charter guarantees the right to have one's cause heard under the conditions of a fair procedure. Under the violation of the right to a fair trial, the Complainant alleges that Mr Benidir's family seized all the competent authorities of the Respondent State and exhausted all local remedies without obtaining satisfactory results. On the basis of the Complainant's arguments, the Commission considers that the examination of a fundamental right, the right to an effective remedy (Article 7(1)(a)), should be retained.

The Commission has considered that "the right to justice entails the obligation for the State to investigate violations, to prosecute their perpetrators and, if their guilt is established, to punish them".

The question that arises in the present case is therefore whether the Respondent State fully discharged its obligation and whether it acted with all due diligence. From the outset, it must be acknowledged that the Respondent State took a series of steps with a view to identifying the perpetrators of the abduction of Mr Benidir, notably by investigating the file and hearing the various persons involved in the case.

However, the examination of the file shows that there were a number of failings in the handling of this case by the national courts, notably the absence of prosecution of the 5 militia members alleged to be the perpetrators of the abduction of Mr Benidir and the length of time taken by the national courts to deal with the case.

The Commission considers that the circumstances of the abduction show that "the patriots" operated in public places and were never troubled by the police. The organisation and mode of operation in places known to the police authorities and with their acquiescence constitute, in the Commission's view, sufficient indications that the Respondent State had every latitude to identify the perpetrators of the enforced disappearance of Ali Benidir. However, no proof was provided by the Respondent State that serious investigations were conducted to shed light on the circumstances and the perpetrators of the abduction, as well as the place of detention or the fate of Ali Benidir. The Commission further notes that of the five "patriots" named as perpetrators of the disappearance, only one appeared once before the courts. For the Commission, the absence of investigation of the persons named as perpetrators of the arrest and disappearance of Benidir represents a breach of a legal duty incumbent on the State which had several means of compelling the alleged perpetrators to appear before the judicial authorities, in this case the use of the warrant to bring a person before the court.

The Commission therefore adopted a decision of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights in the case Velasquez Rodriguez v. Honduras, which considers that governments are required to take reasonable steps to prevent human rights violations and to use the means at their disposal to carry out a serious investigation of violations committed within their territory, identify those responsible, impose the appropriate punishment and ensure the victim adequate compensation.

The Commission further refers to the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights which insists on the State's duty to conduct effective investigations into allegations of human rights violations. In the case Kaya v. Turkey, the Court indeed considered that, having regard to the fundamental importance of the right to life, the right to a remedy implies, in addition to the payment of compensation where appropriate, thorough and effective investigations capable of leading to the identification and punishment of those responsible and entails effective access for the complainant to the investigation procedure.

As regards the Respondent State's argument which affirms that the violations alleged in this communication were adequately dealt with by the national bodies by providing as proof the payment of a monthly compensation pension to the rightful claimants of Benidir Ali, the Commission considers that such a measure in no way affects the established fact of an enforced disappearance and the subsequent violations. As it decided in the case Civil Liberties Organisation v. Nigeria, the Commission recalls that the adoption of alternative measures subsequent to the violation cannot constitute a factor of absolution for the State.

Moreover, the Commission notes that although a judgment of disappearance was rendered by the civil affairs chamber of the Hussein Dey Court on 16 April 2006 in case 2005/4990, the circumstances of the disappearance of Ali Benidir were never clarified by the Algerian courts. In these circumstances, the commission considers that the Respondent State did not discharge its duties arising from Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter to conduct serious investigations aimed at identifying and punishing the perpetrators of the abduction of Ali Benidir and shedding light on his fate.

On the violation of Article 7 with regard to Ordinance No. 06-01, especially its Article 45, the Commission notes that the Complainant alleges the violation of the Benidir family's right to an effective remedy. He puts forward that all the steps undertaken by Ali Benidir's parents after the entry into force of the Ordinance remained in vain because the attorney general of the Hussein Dey Court issued an order of non-suit on 18 April 2006.

The Commission recalls the provisions of Article 45 of the ordinance which provides that "No proceedings may be brought, individually or collectively, against members of any component of the defence and security forces of the Republic, for actions undertaken with a view to protecting persons and property, safeguarding the Nation and preserving the institutions of the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria. Any denunciation or complaint must be declared inadmissible by the competent judicial authority".

The Commission considers that this provision blocks any denunciation or complaint against the alleged perpetrators of human rights violations that occurred during the period of national tragedy, in this case the cases of enforced disappearances.

The Commission considers that requiring the competent judicial authorities to declare any denunciation or complaint inadmissible blocks any domestic judicial step that victims of enforced disappearances that occurred during the period of national tragedy might undertake. The Commission further considers that victims of human rights violations, or members of their families, must have opportunities to be heard and to act in the respective proceedings, both in the steps to clarify the facts and punish those responsible, and in the search for appropriate reparation.

In its normative elaboration of the provisions of the African Charter, the African Commission has considered that general amnesties constituted violations of specific rights guaranteed by the African Charter. Thus, in its General Comment No. 4 on Article 5 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, concerning the right to redress for victims of torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment, the Commission maintains that amnesty laws covering acts of torture are in violation of the right of victims to judicial protection and to have their cause heard under Article 7(1) of the African Charter. The commission further prohibits States from granting general amnesty to persons who have committed acts of torture, especially as such a measure is contrary to the obligation to prosecute the perpetrators and to grant reparation to the victims.

The Commission has also recalled, in its jurisprudence, that by granting total and complete immunity from prosecution which mortgaged access to any remedy that might have been available to victims to vindicate their rights without putting in place alternative legislative or institutional mechanisms guaranteeing that the perpetrators of the alleged atrocities are punished and that the victims of violations are duly compensated or granted other possibilities of seeking an effective remedy, the Respondent State not only prevented victims from seeking reparation but also encouraged impunity and thus reneged on its obligation in violation of Articles 1 and 7(1) of the African Charter.

The Commission has also concluded that amnesty laws cannot exonerate the State that adopts them from its international obligations. It has moreover adopted the position that, by prohibiting the trial of perpetrators of serious human rights violations through amnesties, States would be led to promote not only impunity, but would remove any possibility of investigating these abuses and would deprive the victims of these crimes of an effective remedy for the purpose of obtaining reparations.

The Commission elaborated at length on the question of amnesty in the case Thomas Kwoyelo v. Uganda, recalling that although it is recognised that many types of amnesties are adopted across the world, it should be emphasised that unconditional amnesties not accompanied by measures of accountability are particularly problematic with regard to States' compliance with their international obligations, especially concerning their obligations to respect and protect human rights.

The commission has observed that general or unconditional amnesties which hinder investigations (in particular those concerning the most serious crimes referred to in Article 4(h) of the Constitutive Act of the AU) are not in conformity with the provisions of the African Charter. The Commission emphasised that when African States resort to amnesties as measures necessary to end violence and continuing violations, and to achieve peace and justice, they must respect and honour their regional and international obligations. More particularly, they must ensure that these amnesties meet the essential procedural conditions and must not totally exclude the right of victims to a remedy, in particular remedies taking the form of truth and reparations.

The Commission also recalls that in light of regional and international jurisprudence, amnesty measures (or other measures which enshrine the impunity of the perpetrators of serious crimes) are incompatible with a State's human rights obligations.

In the European system, the European Court of Human Rights has considered that, for the purposes of an effective remedy, it is imperative that criminal proceedings relating to crimes such as torture, which involve serious human rights violations, not be subject to any statute of limitations and that no amnesty or pardon be tolerated in respect of them.

The Inter-American human rights system has a rich jurisprudence relating to national amnesties on account of its historical context where a number of Latin American countries adopted amnesty measures after periods of human rights violations by repressive regimes with the aim of exonerating the perpetrators of these violations from their responsibility.

In this regard, the Inter-American Commission concluded that amnesty laws notably in Argentina, Chile, El Salvador, Haiti, Peru and Uruguay were incompatible with the obligation of States to prosecute serious offences and human rights violations. The American Court goes further and notes that the obligation to investigate and, where appropriate, to prosecute and impose penalties, acquires particular importance in light of the gravity of the crimes committed and the nature of the rights injured, especially taking into account that the prohibition of the enforced disappearance of persons and the correlative duty to investigate and punish those responsible have long since attained the character of jus cogens.

In the same spirit, various African States, through their highest judicial bodies, have recognised the standards in question in respect of their international obligations. Indeed, as observed by the South African Constitutional Court in the case Azania Peoples Organization (AZAPO) v. President of the Republic of South Africa, "every decent human being must feel grave discomfort in living with a decision which allows perpetrators of such abominable atrocities to walk free in the streets of this country". The Court nevertheless distinguished between "[the] decisions taken, by States in transition, in order to foster the achievement of the said transition" and "the acts of a State covering its own crimes by granting itself immunity". In the first case, it is not a matter of government agents who are perpetrators of the violations whitewashing themselves, but rather of a constitutional agreement concluded by all the parties, with the former victims well represented within the framework of an ongoing process, with a view to establishing a constitutional democracy and preventing a repetition of the abuses." This implies that when a country is in transition from a situation of violent internal conflict towards peace and democratic order, the imperative of the transition might require a conditional amnesty and such an amnesty can be considered a legitimate restriction of the right to reparation only when it is: a) formulated with the participation of all sectors of society, in particular the victims, b) approved at the end of a democratic process (by decision of parliament or by referendum), [...] accompanied by alternative measures aimed at redressing the suffering inflicted on the victims.

In the case under examination, the Commission notes the historical context of the drafting and promulgation of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation and its implementing Ordinances and their contribution to the process of peace, national reconciliation and democratisation of the country within the framework of its political transition process. The Commission notes, however, that the Respondent State grants amnesty to State agents but, on the other hand, does not mention any other alternative mechanism for establishing the truth and redressing the suffering inflicted on the victims. The Commission therefore considers that Articles 45 and 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01 undermine the international obligation incumbent on the State to investigate human rights violations because they prevent the victims of the national tragedy or their relatives from filing complaints against the perpetrators of serious human rights violations without providing other remedies; which amounts to granting impunity to the perpetrators.

The Commission further considers that prohibiting recourse to justice is in itself an obstacle to the establishment of the truth because the courts are, in democratic countries, the bodies best equipped to conduct an independent and effective investigation. Although the Commission duly takes into account the fact that the measures identified in the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation are limited to the period of the national tragedy experienced by the country, it also finds that these measures do not offer victims adequate alternative mechanisms.
The Commission concludes from the foregoing that the provisions of Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter have been violated.

The Complainant alleges a violation of Article 9(2) of the Charter in conjunction with Article 1. Article 9(2) of the Charter guarantees the right of every individual to express and disseminate his opinions within the law. Article 1 of the Charter requires States to give effect to the rights, duties and freedoms enshrined in the Charter and to adopt "legislative or other measures" to give effect to them.
The Complainant affirms that Article 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01 constitutes a direct violation of the freedom of expression provided for in Article 9 of the African Charter.

The Commission recalls the content of Article 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01 which provides: "Anyone who, by his statements, writings or any other act, uses or instrumentalises the wounds of the national tragedy, to undermine the institutions of the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria, weaken the State, harm the honourability of its agents who have served it with dignity, or tarnish the image of Algeria internationally, shall be punished by imprisonment of three (3) years to five (5) years and a fine of 250,000 DA to 500,000 DA. Criminal proceedings are initiated ex officio by the public prosecutor's office. In the event of a repeat offence, the penalty provided for in this article is doubled".

The Commission recalls that the right to freedom of expression is a fundamental human right for everyone, which is also the cornerstone of democracy and a means of ensuring respect for all human rights and freedoms. The Commission nevertheless recognises that the exercise of this right carries special responsibilities and duties, which therefore leaves room for certain restrictions or limitations on this right. The Commission considers that restrictions on freedom of expression must be provided by law, in a legitimate interest and necessary in a democratic society. The Commission further recalls that restrictions imposed on freedom of expression must be in conformity with the obligations set out by the Charter and other international human rights standards relating to freedom of expression.

From the arguments developed by the Complainant, it appears that he alleges that Mr Benidir's mother has been prevented from communicating about her grief and distress caused by the disappearance of her son because she risks, under Article 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01, a prison sentence and a fine each time she speaks of her distress or mobilises in a peaceful gathering in favour of truth and justice.

The burden of proving the allegations put forward rests on the Complainant. In the case examined, the Commission finds that the Complainant provides no evidence or material elements in support of the alleged violation.

The Commission is of the view that the mere citation of certain provisions as constituting a violation of the Charter is insufficient to determine a violation of Article 9 against Mr Benidir's mother and relatives. The complainant has the obligation to demonstrate how the contested provisions infringe or have actually infringed the exercise of a victim's human rights. Consequently, the Commission concludes that the alleged violation of Article 9(2) is unfounded.
Article 1 of the African Charter requires States parties to recognise the rights, duties and freedoms enshrined in the Charter and to adopt legislative or other measures to give effect to them.

As noted earlier, the violation of Article 1 of the African Charter can only be established on the condition of the violation of substantive rights and for the provisions whose violation has been found. In the present Communication, the Commission reached the conclusion that the Respondent State violated Articles 4, 5, 6 and 7(1)(a) of the Charter. As a result of the violations of substantive rights thus established, the Commission concludes that there was a violation of Article 1 of the Charter.

The Complainant also alleges that the Respondent State is in violation of Article 1 for having adopted legislative provisions not in conformity with the African Charter, namely Articles 45 and 46 of Ordinance No. 06/01.

The African Commission recalls its decision in the case Amnesty International v. Sudan where it declared that "ratification obliges a State to expedite the harmonisation of its legislation with the provisions of the instrument ratified." It also declared that "Article 1 of the Charter confirms that the government is legally bound to respect the rights and freedoms enshrined in the Charter and to adopt legislation giving effect to them."

In the present case, the African Commission found that the provisions of Articles 45 and 46 of Ordinance No. 06/01 respectively obstruct the right to an effective remedy and freedom of expression and concludes that these articles are contrary to the spirit of Article 1 of the Charter.

In addition to an order declaring the violation of the provisions of the Charter, the Complainant requests the Commission to direct the Respondent State to: - conduct impartial and independent investigations with a view to: ✓ finding Ali Benidir; ✓ bringing the perpetrators of his enforced disappearance before the competent civil authorities; ✓ offering Ali Benidir, if he is still alive, and his mother reparation comprising: • appropriate compensation, proportionate to the gravity of the violation and to the particular circumstances of the case and covering physical and psychological harm, loss of opportunities, including with regard to employment and social benefits, material damage and loss of income, including loss of earning capacity, moral damage and the costs incurred for medicines and medical services; • full and complete rehabilitation comprising medical and psychological care as well as access to legal and social services; • guarantees of non-repetition, in the form notably of the establishment of an independent Commission tasked with shedding full light on the fate of the disappeared and of all the victims of the conflict of the 1990s in Algeria. - respect and give effect to all the international human rights conventions to which it is a party; - amend its legislation in accordance with the rights and freedoms set out in the African Charter, in this case by repealing Articles 45 and 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01.

For the reasons developed above, the Commission finds that there is no need to conclude that the provisions of Article 9(2) of the Charter were violated. It concludes, on the other hand, that the provisions of Articles 1, 4, 5, 6 and 7(1)(a) of the Charter were violated.

The Commission notes, as it has already concluded above, that the file on the disappearance of Mr Benidir Ali was not carefully pursued by the competent judicial authorities. However, the request to find Mr Benidir is unfounded insofar as the Commission itself has already concluded that Mr Benidir is deceased as attested by the documents presented by the Respondent State.

The Complainant requests fair and adequate reparation for the harm suffered by Mr Ali Benidir if he is still alive as well as by his mother. Having concluded that Mr Benidir is no longer of this world, the Commission will address the question of reparation of the harm suffered by his mother.

In accordance with the Commission's established jurisprudence, the violation of rights protected by the Charter gives rise to a right to reparation, including monetary reparation. It has further observed that even if the purpose of damages in human rights litigation need not necessarily be punitive, money can heal wounds. The commission considers, however, that no financial compensation can redeem human lives lost.

The Commission notes that the Complainant did not determine the amount of this reparation. It positively assesses the efforts made by the Respondent State with a view to restoring peace and national concord. It further notes the measures taken by the Respondent State with a view to compensating the relatives of the victims of the national tragedy, including the relatives of Ali Benidir, namely; his mother Houria Berkane, his wife Boudahane Nadjat and his daughter Benidir Anfal, who receive a monthly pension of 16,000 DA (equivalent to 147 US dollars) and have done so since 2007.

The Commission observes that although the present Communication concerns only the case of Mr Benidir and his family, it is a matter of public interest and the Respondent State has for years been carrying out a general compensation of the victims of the national tragedy. It recalls that reparation may be made by individual or collective compensation. It may also be made in a symbolic manner. This is the case in Communication 318/06 – Open Society Justice Initiative v. Côte d'Ivoire, in which the Commission considered that in view of the large number of victims and the nature of the rights concerned, material or monetary reparation was not appropriate and prescribed symbolic compensation and the immediate adoption of administrative, legislative, regulatory and practical measures to put an end to the violations and prevent them from recurring in the future.

In view of the large number of victims concerned by the national tragedy, and duly taking into account the fact that informed and aware citizens, in this case the mother of Mr Benidir, agreed to adhere to the compensation provisions which they receive monthly under the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation, the Commission concludes that it is fair for the State to continue the compensation granted to the victims within the framework of the implementation of the Charter.

The Commission recognises that the disappearance of Mr Benidir caused moral suffering to the victim's relatives. It considers well-founded the request for medical and psychological care as well as access to legal and social services. It is therefore appropriate to order that the Respondent State grant medical and psychological support to Mr Benidir's mother if she so requests. The Respondent State must also guarantee her adequate legal support with a view to pursuing the necessary judicial remedies.

The Commission concludes that the lack of due diligence to shed light on the human rights violations perpetrated against Mr Benidir did not allow his relatives to know the truth about what really happened. As noted supra, the present Communication pertains to public interest litigation whose outcome will have an impact on the other victims of the national tragedy. The Commission is therefore of the view that the establishment of an independent Commission tasked with shedding light on the events that occurred during the period of the national tragedy will make it possible to respond to the quest for truth sought by the victims. Respect for and implementation of all the international human rights conventions to which the Respondent State is a party.

In view of the conclusions of the analysis of the Communication, the request relating to respect for the implementation of the international conventions ratified is well-founded and the Commission recommends that the State party promote, protect and implement the rights guaranteed by the duly ratified human rights instruments.

The Commission has concluded that the content of Articles 45 and 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01 is not in conformity with the African Charter and the other relevant conventions to which Algeria is a party. These provisions violate the right to an effective remedy because they prevent any injured person from filing a complaint against members of the defence and security forces, for actions undertaken with a view to protecting persons and preserving national institutions. They further violate the right to freedom of expression because they provide for sanctions up to imprisonment for anyone who uses or instrumentalises the wounds of the national tragedy. Consequently, it is appropriate to recommend that the Respondent State amend the two articles with a view to their conformity with the African Charter and other relevant human rights instruments.

In light of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights: a. Finds that the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria did not violate the provisions of Article 9(2); b. Finds on the other hand that the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria violated the provisions of Articles 1, 4, 5, 6 and 7(1)(a) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights; c. Requests the Respondent State to take the appropriate measures to: ✓ Conduct a thorough, rigorous and independent investigation into the facts of the present Communication in order to determine the various responsibilities and provide the family of the disappeared person with detailed information on the results of the investigations; ✓ Effectively apply, against the alleged culprits, the penalties provided for by law; ✓ Continue the payment of the compensation granted to Ali Benidir's mother as reparation for the moral harm suffered; ✓ Grant the necessary legal, medical and psychological support to Ali Benidir's mother; ✓ Put in place a transitional justice mechanism to respond to the imperatives of the right to truth and of the fight against impunity; ✓ Amend the provisions of Articles 45 and 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01 of 27 February 2006 implementing the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation in conformity with the relevant provisions of the Charter; d. Requests the Respondent State to report to it in writing, within one hundred and eighty (180) days from the notification of the present decision, on the measures taken for the implementation of these recommendations. Adopted at the 24th Extraordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, held from 30 July to 8 August 2018 in Banjul, The Gambia.

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat), received a complaint on 15 December 2014 from Peter Odiwuor Ngoge (the Complainant), representing himself and his clients, John Mwangi Muhia, Charles Muema, and Bronx Estate Limited (the Victims), against the Republic of Kenya (Respondent State), a State Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).
The Complainant submits that he is an advocate of the High Court of Kenya, and practices in the law firm O. P. Ngoge & Associates.

The Complainant submits that on 08 June 2012 the Victims, represented by the Complainant, filed a constitutional petition (No. 269) seeking the intervention of the High Court of Kenya for enforcement of their fundamental human rights, which they claimed to have been violated by the Director of Public Prosecutions and four other Respondents. The alleged violations include the arrest and detention of Mr Muhia for the alleged offence of breaking and entering and stealing the hotel goods of the fourth Respondent, as well as setting the bail at an "unconscionable and unreasonable" amount and the attempt to execute the committal orders against both Mr Muhia and Mr Muema, for alleged contempt of the orders of the Business Premises Tribunal issued on 02 December 2011 (execution of which had been stayed, according to the Complainant, on 05 January 2012).

The Complainant alleges that Justice Mumbi Ngugi on 25 September 2012 halted the hearing of the constitutional petition of 08 June 2012 and postponed it indefinitely to give the Attorney-General and the Respondents' advocates time to file their responses belatedly. The petition was listed for mention for further directions on 15 October 2012.

The Complainant avers that on 15 October 2012 Justice Ngugi did not sit and instead, Justice Majanja directed that the case be relisted for mention on 02 November 2012 before Justice Ngugi. However, the Complainant claims that the Respondent's advocates who were present in court on 15 October 2012 deliberately failed to serve him with a mention Notice and that the Deputy Registrar also did not issue a mention Notice for him to attend court on 02 November 2012. However, the mention did not take place on 02 November 2012, and the Complainant submits that the case was instead listed on 05 November 2012, again without his knowledge. The Complainant further submits that upon ex parte hearing of the Respondents on 05 November 2012, Justice Ngugi issued a further mention date for 19 November 2012 which the Respondents also failed to serve on the Complainant, again resulting in his absence.

The Complainant claims that on 19 November 2012 Justice Ngugi arbitrarily directed that the Complainant should come to court on 03 December 2012 to explain why the petition should not be dismissed for want of prosecution. The Justice instructed the Deputy Registrar to give notice of this to the Complainant, and while the notice was issued on 20 November 2012, the Complainant avers that it was not served on him and that no affidavit of service was filed on record to confirm service of the notice.

The Complainant submits that Justice Ngugi on 03 December 2012 proceeded to dismiss the case with costs to the Respondents without delving into the merits of the constitutional petition, and without first satisfying herself that the notice to show case dated 20 November 2012 had been properly served on the Complainant.

The Complainant submits that, aggrieved by this decision, he filed the Notice of Motion dated 29 July 2013 seeking the intervention of the High Court to set aside the ex parte orders of 03 December 2012 and re-admit the constitutional petition. This Notice of Motion was dismissed on 17 October 2013. Thereupon the Complainant lodged civil appeal No. 337 of 2013, civil appeal No. 339 of 2013 and civil application No. NAI 307 of 2013 in the Kenyan Court of Appeal in November 2013 with the aim of overturning the dismissal orders of 03 December 2012 and 17 October 2013, restoring the original 08 June 2012 constitutional petition to a hearing on merits and staying the criminal proceedings emanating from the decision of the Business Premises Tribunal. These civil appeals and application were still pending undetermined by the Court of Appeal at the time of the submission of this Complaint to the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission).

The Complainant avers that the Respondent State curtailed the provisions of the African Charter by permitting Justice Ngugi to dismiss the aforesaid constitutional petition, thereby exposing the Victims to unlawful arrest, criminal prosecution and loss of business arising out of the orders of the Business Premises Rent Tribunal in case No. 806 of 2011. The Complainant further avers that these violations are exacerbated by the undue delay of the Court of Appeal to set-down the above mentioned civil appeals for urgent hearings and disposal.

The Complainant further alleges that the Respondent State permitted Justice Ngugi to allow advocates of the Respondents to fix ex parte hearing or mention dates of the constitutional petition without the Complainant's involvement and to also dismiss the aforesaid constitutional petition in violation of various provisions of the rules published by the Chief Justice of Kenya, the Civil Procedure Rules of 2010, and the Constitution of Kenya, thereby subjecting the Complainant and the Victims to unfair and unlawful treatment, discrimination and condemnation contrary to the provisions of the African Charter.

Through the unlawful dismissal of the constitutional petition, the Complainant alleges, Justice Ngugi deliberately created a rift of misunderstanding between the Complainant and his clients (the Victims) which could trigger a complaint against him, and which the Law Society of Kenya would use to disbar him from legal practice in violation of his socio-economic rights.

The Complainant avers that the deliberate dismissal of the petition was part of the widespread unlawful treatment, intimidation, harassment, and economic sanctions his firm is being subjected to by the Respondent State with the aim of crippling his legal practice as a punishment in retribution following previous exposure by him of official wrongdoings in his capacity as a human rights defender.

The Complainant submits that he has lodged the Complaint with the Commission because local judicial remedies are not effectively available to him and to his clients and that such local remedies cannot be pursued without hindrances, owing to mistrust and lack of professional respect between him and the Judiciary of the Respondent State.
The Complainant also indicates that the petition has never been presented before any other international dispute settlement forum or before any other treaty body for settlement or adjudication.
The Complainant alleges violation of Articles 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12, 15, 19, 22, and 24 of the African Charter.

The Complainant requests the Commission to: a. Request reparations in the form of general damages of Kenya shillings 10 billion to be assessed and awarded to the Victims to redress violations of their fundamental human rights; b. Request that the Respondent be blocked or restrained from pursuing the criminal prosecutions against the Victim arising from the orders of the Business Premises Rent Tribunal case; c. Request that general damages of Kenya shillings 300 billion be assessed and awarded to the Complainant for the deprivation of effective local judicial remedies; and d. Request payment of interest on (a) and (c) above and costs of the petition.
The Secretariat received the Complaint on 15 December 2014 and acknowledged receipt of the same on 17 March 2015.
The Commission considered the Complaint during its 18 Extra-Ordinary Session held from 29 July to 07 August 2015 and decided to be seized of the matter.
By correspondences of 12 August 2015 the Secretariat transmitted the seizure decision to the parties and requested the Complainant to submit on admissibility within sixty (60) days.

On 02 December 2015 the Complainant's submissions on admissibility were received at the Secretariat, which were subsequently forwarded to the Respondent State on 08 December 2015 requesting the latter to submit their written submissions on admissibility within sixty (60) days. The Complainant submitted his admissibility submissions together with the admissibility submissions for three other Communications pending before the Commission, from which is it possible to ascertain that he submitted the same submissions on all four Communications.
On 17 December 2015 the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Respondent State acknowledged receipt of the Complainant's submissions on admissibility.
On 06 January 2016 a second copy of the same submissions by the Complainant on admissibility reached the Commission, of which the Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 8 March 2016.

On 08 March 2016 by Ref: ACHPR/COM/524/15/KEN/387/16 the Secretariat transmitted the Complainant's submissions on admissibility to the Respondent State for the second time. The submissions were received by the Respondent State on 21 March 2016 according to DHL tracking records.

On 18 May 2016 by Note Verbale Ref: ACHPR/COM/524/15/KEN/1007/16 and letter Ref: ACHPR/COM/524/15/KEN/1006/16 the Secretariat informed the Parties that the Communication was deferred during the 58 Ordinary Session of the Commission.

On 21 July 2016 by letter Ref: ACHPR/COM/524/15/KEN/1386/16 and Note Verbale Ref: ACHPR/COM/524/15/KEN/1385/16 the Secretariat informed the Parties that the Respondent State would be granted an extension of thirty (30) days within which to submit their overdue submissions on admissibility.

On 22 November 2016 by letter Ref: ACHPR/COM/524/15/KEN/1836/16 and Note Verbale Ref: ACHPR/COM/524/15/KEN/1837/16 the Secretariat informed the Parties that the deadline for submissions by the Respondent State was 25 August 2016 and that the Commission will proceed to decide on admissibility based on information received within the timelines stipulated.
Consideration of the admissibility of the Communication was subsequently deferred until the present 23 Extra-Ordinary Session of the Commission.

The Complainant submits that in Jawara vs. The Gambia, the Commission formulated three major criteria for admission of Communications for hearing on merit; that is the local remedy must be available, effective and sufficient. The Complainant further submits that a remedy is considered available if the petitioner can pursue it without impediment and is sufficient if it is capable of redressing the complaint.

Furthermore, the Complainant submits that if the applicant cannot turn to the Judiciary in his country because of a generalized fear for his life, local remedies would be considered to be unavailable to him.

The Complainant avers that local remedies are either unavailable, insufficient or not effective at all and cannot therefore be accessed freely by him without coming into contact with artificial impediments, hindrances and hurdles placed on the Complainant's way, which barriers are utilized by agents of the Respondent State to impede the Complainant as a legal practitioner and to the detriment of his clientele.

The Complainant further avers that the ruling of the Vetting of Judges & Magistrates Board of Kenya, delivered on 25 April 2012, constitutes an express and unequivocal official public admission on the part of the Respondent State to the effect that local remedies are either unavailable, insufficient or are not effectively accessible at all by the Complainant and his clientele, without coming face to face with artificial impediments unlawfully erected on the way by agents of the Respondent State to impede or delay access to justice. The Complainant avers that this is because the Vetting Board did not utilise the information supplied to it by the Complainant in order to remove or vet out recalcitrant judicial officers, thereby exposing the Complainant and his clients to revenge, retribution and retaliation by the said judicial officers as well as retribution from their friends, sympathizers and colleagues in the Government of the Respondent State, the Bar and the Bench.

The Complainant submits that he submitted complaints to the Judicial Service Commission of Kenya, the Office of the Chief Justice, the Vetting of Judges and Magistrates Board of Kenya, the Office of the former Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs, the Office of the Attorney General, the Office of the Government Ombudsman, the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights and to the Law Society of Kenya.
