The Commission further notes that since the seizure of the Supreme Court, the investigation of the file has remained at the same stage and that no follow-up has been given to the Complainants after one year and eight months of proceedings. In these circumstances, the Commission must conclude that local remedies have been unduly prolonged.

Turning to the effectiveness of the remedies, it may readily be deduced from the foregoing that the remedies having thus been prolonged could manifestly not be effective. Moreover, the Commission notes in particular that the acts complained of by the authors of the present Communication are attributed to the President of the Republic, head of the executive power. Under the applicable Congolese law, the President of the Republic is also President of the Higher Council of the Judiciary, the body in charge of the management of magistrates' careers. Furthermore, the President of the Republic appoints the magistrates but also the President of the Supreme Court, the court which hears the application lodged by the Complainants.

In view of these considerations, the Commission is of the opinion that the prerogatives thus conferred on the head of the executive power in the management of the judicial power are likely to influence the normal course of effective local remedies. Such a possibility should constitute an additional reason for the administration of prompt justice. Considering in this instance the time taken by the Supreme Court to follow up on the Complainants' applications, the Commission considers that justice being the citizen's last resort, its administration must be characterised by a certain speed. Obviously, the procedure before the Supreme Court was not the subject of such speed in the present case. Consequently, the Commission finds that local remedies were not effective, without there being any further need to rule on whether they were satisfactory.

In any event, on the question of the exhaustion of local remedies, the Commission finds that the said remedies exist in this case but that they were prolonged and could therefore not be effective. Consequently, it is for the Commission to conclude that the Complainants must be exempted from the exhaustion of local remedies.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the present Communication admissible in accordance with the provisions of Article 56 of the African Charter.

In addition to the provisions whose violation they allege at the admissibility stage, the Complainants present, at the merits stage, arguments seeking to have the violation of the provisions of Articles 3, 18 and 26 of the Charter found. On the other hand, they do not make submissions on Article 16 whose violation they had alleged in the Complaint.

The Complainants allege that their dismissal by the President of the Republic violates the provisions of Article 26 in that it was decreed in disregard of the procedure prescribed by national law and the international guidelines in this matter. They thus report that the procedure provided for before the Higher Council of the Judiciary was not followed and that the magistrates were not heard despite all the steps they undertook to that end.

According to the Complainants, the acts of dismissal are also ill-founded in law. In this regard, they put forward that the Orders made to ground the dismissal originate from convictions in prise à partie dating from more than a year ago in violation of the Constitution and the Law on the statute of the judiciary. They consider that even on the assumption that the magistrates would not be covered by this limitation period, the dismissal Orders do not mention at any point a disciplinary procedure against them.

In support of this allegation, the Complainants put forward the absence of a fair procedure during which they should have been heard and had the opportunity to defend themselves. In addition to the violation of the right to be heard, they allege that the responses of the various authorities to their attempts to have the impugned decisions annulled violate their right to a remedy. They report that the remedies undertaken before the President of the Republic and the Administrative Section of the Supreme Court of Justice remained without follow-up.

Furthermore, the Complainants maintain that their massive and arbitrary dismissal deprives those seeking justice of qualified personnel and consequently of the right to have their cause heard by a competent court.
The Complainants allege that the dismissal resulted in the loss of their jobs, obliging them to take part in any type of economic activity.

According to the Complainants, the right to work is indispensable to the exercise of other human rights, notably those linked to survival. They allege that consequently the right to work is inseparable from the right to dignity of which it is an integral part so that the deprivation of the former undermines the latter.

The Complainants conclude that their dignity was violated as a result of the fact that, deprived of their means of survival, they live in total destitution, with wives and children in their charge. Some of them are said to have died as a result of the depression caused by their situation. They allege psychological suffering intentionally inflicted to intimidate them and obtain their subservience to the Executive power.
The Complainants allege that the violation of Articles 5, 7 and 15 of the African Charter automatically entails that of the provisions of the articles whose violation is alleged here.

As regards Article 17 of the Charter, they put forward that, read in tandem with the articles of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child, its violation is established as a result of the loss of the source of income which served to provide for the education, housing and food of their children.

As for Article 18, its violation would be established by the fact that the Respondent State dismissed them without taking the necessary precautions to minimise the consequences on the lives and survival of their families, of the children in particular.

To support this allegation, the Complainants put forward the difference in treatment they suffered. They report that the Presidency of the Republic, the Supreme Court of Justice and the Higher Council of the Judiciary received the applications of other dismissed magistrates and examined them whereas all their attempts to the same end were doomed to failure. They cite one of their colleagues, Mwanga Mukudi, who was reinstated and appointed to a new post following their dismissal.

According to the Complainants, despite having put in place the legislative framework necessary for respect of the rights whose violation is alleged, the Respondent State failed in its obligation under the provisions of Article 1. They maintain in this regard that the State failed to translate normative protection into effective enjoyment in that both the informal and the judicial remedies were obstructed. They report in particular the remedies undertaken in 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013 and 2014 without the slightest response from the competent authorities of the Respondent State.

As the procedure expressly indicates, the Respondent State did not transmit its observations on the merits despite the correspondence that the Secretariat addressed to it in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Rules of Procedure.

In accordance with the provisions of Rule 105(1) of its Rules of Procedure, the Parties each have a period of sixty (60) days to transmit their submissions on the merits. They also have, upon their express request, an additional period not exceeding thirty (30) days per party at each stage of the procedure. The Secretariat ensures the exchange of pleadings and the observance of these various time limits.

In the present case, the Commission notes that these procedural prescriptions were indeed observed. In this instance, upon the expiry of the initial period of sixty (60) days, the Respondent State did not submit a request for an additional period. However, due to time constraints and the cancellation of its 56th Ordinary Session initially scheduled to be held in October 2014, the Commission deferred the examination of the Communication to its successive sessions. The State consequently benefited from an implicit additional period of eleven (11) months in addition to the two (02) months provided for by the Rules of Procedure.

Furthermore, on 16 March 2015, the Secretariat addressed a reminder correspondence to the Respondent State, following the decision adopted by the Commission at its 17th Extraordinary Session (February 2015) to grant a final period of one month to the Parties that had not submitted their observations upon the expiry of the time limits provided for by the Rules of Procedure. Despite this correspondence sent by DHL courier, the Respondent State did not submit the required observations. Consequently, the Commission decides to examine the Communication on the basis of the elements in its possession, in accordance with its practice.
The Commission notes that the Complainants do not make submissions on Article 16 whose violation they had alleged in the Complaint. It is appropriate to find a withdrawal in this regard.

On the request for extension of arguments, the Commission notes that it is not based on new facts, is covered by the decision on admissibility and is substantiated by the Complainants. Despite the fact that the Respondent State is in default, the Commission in judging by default, ensures the merit of the arguments put forward by the Complainant.

Article 26 of the Charter mainly prescribes to the Respondent State to guarantee the independence of the courts. In the case Meldrum v. Zimbabwe, the Commission concluded that the independence of the courts necessarily presupposes the absence of pressure or interference. As regards the assessment of this independence, it took the position in Wetsh'okonda Koso and Others v. Democratic Republic of the Congo that the independence of the courts must in any event be assessed with regard to the executive power. As criteria of assessment, the Commission retained, among others, appointment, security of tenure, protection against external pressures and the perception of independence. Furthermore, and very notably, the Commission concluded that the judiciary lacked independence in Gunme and Others v. Cameroon on the finding that the Higher Council of the Judiciary was chaired by the President of the Republic assisted by the Minister of Justice.

The Commission considers that in democratic regimes based on the rule of law and where the functioning of systems of government is governed by the separation of powers, the independence of the judge should be assessed in light of the adage "justice must not only be done, it must also be seen to be done". The European Court of Human Rights goes in this direction when it constantly relies on the conduct of the executive to assess compliance by judicial authorities with the presumption of innocence. In Konstas v. Greece for example, the Court concludes that public statements by members of the government, mainly the minister of justice, necessarily give the public the impression that there is interference with the course of justice.

Likewise, the European Court of Human Rights holds, notably in the leading decisions Medvedyev v. France and Moulin v. France, that the public prosecutor is disqualified from exercising judicial functions notably for lack of independence vis-à-vis the executive power.

The Commission recognises that in the constitutional order of modern States, the day-to-day conduct of public affairs may logically require that the executive power be vested with certain appointment functions without however this being an opportunity for the vassalisation of the other powers, notably the Judiciary, at the risk of a violation of the separation of powers. In such an order, what must prevail is the purpose of the functions assigned, that is the regular functioning of State institutions, and not the opportunity for interference by one power in another.

In this regard, the United Nations Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary are more than relevant. It is appropriate in this instance to cite Principle 19 under which "All disciplinary, suspension or removal proceedings shall be determined in accordance with established standards of judicial conduct". It is in the same logic that the constitutional guarantees of independence of the judge against the executive must be understood, notably principles such as irremovability and prior consultation before appointment or assignment. The merit of this is that the functional powers granted to the executive are necessarily understood as having to be rigorously circumscribed in order to preserve one of the main determinants of the separation of powers which is the independence of the judiciary.

In the present case, the Commission notes that the domestic law of the Respondent State clearly provides for such guarantees in that Organic Law No. 06/020 of 10 October 2006 on the statute of magistrates unequivocally prescribes that disciplinary procedures with respect to magistrates must necessarily precede a request for dismissal which, for its part, may be requested only by the Higher Council of the Judiciary (CSM). Furthermore, even the proposal for dismissal made by the CSM must respect certain rules including, in this instance, the right to defence, notification of the documents in the file and proof of appearance before the Council.

The elements contained in the file indicate that the Complainants were never heard, much less by the CSM, and were informed of their dismissal and of the facts alleged against them only through the press. Nor did they receive notification of the dismissal Orders and of the documents in the file.

Moreover, the dismissal Orders were based on a conviction in prise à partie before the Supreme Court of Justice whereas under domestic law, such a procedure is civil and not disciplinary and only a disciplinary procedure can entail a disciplinary sanction such as dismissal. The Commission notes that by an attempt to regularise the incriminated acts, the executive hastened to have Parliament enact a law making conviction in prise à partie a disciplinary offence punishable by dismissal.

The Commission notes moreover that despite the fact that the Respondent State undertook reforms putting an end to the participation of the executive power in the functioning of the judicial power through the Higher Council of the Judiciary, the powers of appointment and dismissal have remained. In light of recent developments crystallised by the jurisprudence recalled above, the use that the President of the Republic made of the said powers is at odds with the realisation of the separation of powers and the independence of the judiciary.

In the circumstances of the case, it was indispensable that measures of direct intervention by the executive power in the functioning of the judicial power be marked by the subtlety and consideration most respectful of the sacrosanct principle of the separation of powers. This was not the case. Consequently, it must be concluded, without any need to examine the subsequent arguments, that the incriminated acts violate the provisions of Article 26 of the Charter.

From the arguments invoked by the Complainants, it emerges that they allege the violation of the right to have one's cause heard. The provisions at issue are therefore those of Article 7(1) of the Charter. They further maintain that the massive dismissal of magistrates violates the same right with regard to those seeking justice and users of justice.

The Commission refers to the substance of its numerous precedents on the right to be heard as a primary component of the fair trial. The Complainants have proved that they were never heard prior to their dismissal whereas the law required it. All their subsequent attempts to be heard in accordance with the procedures established by the Respondent State itself remained without follow-up for more than two years. The Commission concludes that the provisions of Article 7(1) of the Charter have been violated.

Under the provisions of Article 15, "Every individual shall have the right to work under equitable and satisfactory conditions, and shall receive equal pay for equal work". The acts incriminated in the present case amount to an unlawful dismissal and consequently a deprivation of the right to work which is not in conformity with law and justice.

The Commission's findings regarding the allegations of violation of Article 26 of the Charter amply establish the unlawful nature of the Complainants' dismissal. In its jurisprudence on the right to work, the Commission considers that such a right covers access to employment, security in employment and reinstatement unless appropriate compensation is paid.

The Commission thus concluded in Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and Associated Newspapers of Zimbabwe v. Zimbabwe, that the fact for the Respondent State of closing the Complainants' offices and preventing their employees from going there deprives them of a source of income and consequently violates Article 15 of the Charter. It concluded to a violation of the same provisions when, in Pagnoulle (on behalf of Mazou) v. Cameroon, the Respondent State refused to reinstate the Complainant in his functions as magistrate whereas all the persons who had been the subject of convictions like him had been reinstated.

In the present case, the dismissal was unlawful including with respect to the relevant law of the Respondent State. Being magistrates by training, the Complainants were deprived of exercising a highly specialised function for which they had been trained. The loss of such employment and the improbability of being able to exercise functions as specific as those of judging unquestionably establish an impediment to enjoying the right to work under the provisions of Article 15 of the Charter. Moreover, the attempts to be reinstated in their jobs were unsuccessful. The Commission concludes to the violation of Article 15 of the Charter.

By the arguments they invoke in support of the allegation of violation of Article 5, the Complainants mainly target the right to human dignity and the prohibition of degrading treatment. The Commission considers that, just as work ensures independence, it guarantees dignity. Such an interpretation of the scope of the right to work is confirmed by the United Nations Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights which considers that this right "is essential for realizing other human rights and forms an inseparable and inherent part of human dignity".

In the present case, the Complainants were dismissed on the basis of Orders ill-founded in both fact and law. Furthermore, instead of the formal notification provided for by law, they learned of the Orders and of the reasons motivating them through the press. This already tarnishes the honour and dignity of magistrates supposed to embody the judicial power in the eyes of the public. In any event, the fact of having been deprived of their employment unlawfully and in the circumstances of the case placed the Complainants in a state of indignity.

On the ground of the existence of inhuman treatment and torture, the Commission concluded, in the cases Modise v. Botswana and Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and Interights v. Egypt, that inhuman and degrading treatment necessarily violates human dignity. It must be considered that the reverse is possible in that indignity is already necessarily inhuman.

In the case under examination, it is noted that the loss of their employment placed the Complainants in an economic situation marked by material destitution. For heads of family with spouses and children in their charge, the ensuing psychological suffering is logical. As put forward by the Complainants, some of them suffered from depression and several deaths were recorded as a result of illness.

To prove torture, the Complainants allege intimidation and the desire for subservience to the executive power as the purposes pursued. The Commission notes that torture must, to be established, involve a certain degree of suffering even if it is psychological. In the present case, this proof is not sufficiently made any more than the alleged objective of intimidation has been proved. If the Commission cannot conclude to torture, it must, on the other hand, be found that the incriminated acts are degrading. The provisions of Article 5 of the Charter have consequently been violated. On the alleged violation of Articles 17 and 18 of the Charter, read together with Articles 17, 18, 19 and 20 of the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACRWC)

On the basis of the Charter, the Complainants allege the violation of the rights to education (Article 17 of the Charter), to the protection of the physical health and moral of the family (Article 18 of the Charter), read together with the rights not to be subjected to inhuman treatment (Article 17 ACRWC), to the protection of the family (Article 18 ACRWC), to parental care and protection (Article 19 ACRWC), to parental and State assistance regarding nutrition, health, education, clothing and housing (Article 20 ACRWC).

The Commission notes that it does not have jurisdiction ratione materiae to hear allegations of violations of the provisions of the ACRWC for which the Committee of Experts set up in this regard has exclusive charge of the contentious matters. That said, and on the basis of the provisions of Article 60 of the Charter, the Commission may, in interpreting the provisions of Articles 17 and 18 of the Charter invoked, draw inspiration from the ACRWC. Furthermore, the ACRWC being an instrument of the African system adopted subsequent to the Charter, it is relevant to seek in the later and much more detailed instrument, the scope of rights briefly set out in the earlier instrument. In the event that failures to comply with the provisions of Articles 17 and 18 of the African Charter are established, the Commission will therefore retain only the violation of the provisions of the said articles alone and not that of the provisions of the ACRWC.

The provisions concerned having all been recalled supra, there is no need to dwell on their meaning and scope. It will suffice to note that in the present case, the Complainants suddenly dismissed from their functions had families in their charge, including children whom they said were of school age. The care and protection guaranteed to the family and the child by the aforementioned provisions are necessarily compromised when the family member who provides the resources is deprived of his livelihood as is the case here.

The facts dating from 2009, and the magistrates never having been reinstated, their families have borne the consequence of their dismissal for a period of nearly seven years. This state of affairs seriously undermines the physical and moral well-being of the child, the woman and the entire family. The absence of an effective response and of reparatory measures adds to the suffering thus endured by the Complainants. The Commission therefore concludes to the violation of Articles 17 and 18 of the Charter.

Article 3 of the Charter guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the law. The Complainants allege the absence of equal protection of the law on the basis of the reinstatement of one of the magistrates who had been dismissed in the same circumstances.

In Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and Another v. Zimbabwe the Commission interprets equal protection of the law as that of every person to have equal access to the courts and to be treated equally by them both in procedure and in substance. There is therefore, in the essence of this right, an implicit guarantee of non-discrimination in judicial proceedings and in the application of the law to persons in the same conditions.

In Meldrum v. Zimbabwe cited supra, the Commission thus requires the Respondent State to prove the absence of differentiated treatment in order to refute the allegation of violation of Article 3(2) of the Charter. The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice adopts the same position when in the case Essien v. The Gambia, it considers that the right protected under Article 15 refers both to the prerogative of accessing employment as a source of income and of benefiting, in a work situation, from the same treatment as persons in similar circumstances.

In the present Communication, the Complainants seized respectively the President of the Republic and the Supreme Court of Justice. They further lodged a request for reinstatement before the CSM without success. While these requests had all been ignored, the President of the Republic proceeded to the reinstatement and appointment of magistrate Mwanga Mukudi to the rank of permanent judge of the Commercial Court. The said magistrate had been dismissed by the same incriminated Orders in the same circumstances as the Complainants. Such treatment violates the provisions of Article 3(2) of the Charter. 29. According to the Complainants, despite having made the informal remedies available, the State failed to guarantee their enjoyment since the said remedies remained without follow-up. In this regard, the Commission refers to its jurisprudence to note that, in principle, non-observance of the obligation prescribed in Article 1 is established once a violation of a provision of the Charter is found. 30. That said, the Commission observes that the obligation arising from the provisions of Article 1 of the Charter is twofold in that it is both an obligation of means and of result. In the present case, the Commission notes that the former has been fulfilled given that the remedies are provided for by law. On the other hand, it appears that the impossibility of enjoying the remedies through lack of response entails a failure of the Respondent State with respect to the obligation of result. In these circumstances, it must be concluded that the provisions of Article 1 of the Charter have been violated.

The Commission having heard the Complainants on all of their arguments, it is appropriate to examine the related requests. The said requests mostly amount to administrative actions and pecuniary compensation. These categories of reparation are established in the practice of the Commission in application of the provisions of the Charter.

On the request for reinstatement, the Commission notes that the findings of violation and the unlawful nature found of the acts of dismissal must annihilate their effect. Inasmuch as the Respondent State has undertaken no procedure to establish misconduct or unfitness to exercise the functions of magistrate, it is appropriate to require outright reinstatement with all the legal consequences. The ensuing damages must include the salaries and benefits owed, all other resulting losses as well as reparation for moral prejudice.

As to public acknowledgement and solemn apologies, the Commission observes that the functions of such a type of reparation are multiple. Such apologies may aim at the psychological healing of victims, the promotion of social justice, the restoration of social balance or seek to induce a change in behaviour. It emerges from its application that the importance of apologies in the victim's understanding and perception of them must be taken into account. In general, the public image of the victim has been damaged, which may explain the frequent recourse to this mode of reparation in cases of defamation. The choice of means and actors for the implementation of this reparation is also key to its effectiveness.

In the present case, the Commission concluded that the honour and dignity of the Complainants were tarnished in the eyes of the public. Furthermore, the independence of the judiciary and the separation of powers constitute constitutional principles of public interest. Their violation is likely to diminish in the eyes of the public, the perception of trust that it must have with regard to the courts, the judges and justice. Where applicable, it is necessary to remedy these ruptures by public statements.

Legislative measures with a view to preventing infringements of the independence of the judiciary by the executive power must necessarily involve a thorough reform of the system of judicial organisation and respect for the separation of powers. These principles being established by the Constitution, it is appropriate to require that it be brought into conformity with the provisions of Articles 7 and 26 of the Charter. The Commission, For these reasons,

Finds that the Democratic Republic of the Congo has violated the provisions of Articles 1, 3, 5, 7(1), 15, 17, 18 and 26 of the Charter. Consequently: i. Requests the Democratic Republic of the Congo to take all necessary diligent measures for the reinstatement of the Complainants with all the legal consequences. ii. Requests the Democratic Republic of the Congo to pay the Complainants the amounts corresponding to the salaries and other benefits owed for the time elapsed since the dismissal. iii. Further requests the Democratic Republic of the Congo to pay the Complainants just damages for the moral prejudice suffered as a result of the violations found. iv. Further requests the Democratic Republic of the Congo to present public apologies to the Complainants as well as to Congolese citizens seeking justice for the violation of the independence of the judiciary and of access to justice. The said apologies shall be presented by a member of the government of the Respondent State. v. Also requests the Democratic Republic of the Congo to take all legislative or other measures with a view to guaranteeing at all times the independence of the judiciary in conformity with the provisions of domestic law and of Articles 7 and 26 of the Charter. vi. Finally requests the Democratic Republic of the Congo to report to it in writing, within five eighty (180) days of notification of the present decision, on the measures undertaken with a view to implementing these recommendations. Adopted on 16 February 2016 at the 19th Extraordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights held from 16 to 25 February 2016 in Banjul, The Gambia.

The Complaint is brought against the Republic of Kenya (the Respondent State) by the Kenyan Section of the International Commission of Jurists - ICJ Kenya (Complainant) on behalf of, and for the benefit of Kenyans, especially those resident in the Mount Elgon District of Kenya.

The Complainant alleges that between 2006 and 2008, State Security Agents of the Respondent State "jointly and/or severally with other non-state actors" carried out executions, acts of torture, cruelty, inhuman and degrading treatment against thousands of Kenyan citizens (the Victims) who were resident in the Mount Elgon District. Most of the Victims allegedly come from the Sabaot, Teso and Busuku ethnic communities that make up the population of the Mount Elgon District.

Between 1965 and 1971, the Complainant alleges further, the Respondent State decided to resettle the Dorobos (a sub-group of the Sabaot) in the lower parts of Mount Elgon. This move led to a series of events that included the springing up of land disputes and also resulted in the emergence of an armed militia group known as the Sabaot Land Defence Force (SLDF). The Complainant states that the SLDF got involved in terrorising and executing the Victims between 2005 and 2007, culminating in the 2008 post-election violence in Kenya.

The Complainant alleges that, the Respondent State deployed joint-security forces to the Mount Elgon District area in an operation code-named "Okoa Maisha" and that the Security Agents of the Respondent State during this operation "jointly and severally" executed tortured or treated residents of Mount Elgon cruelly and inhumanely. The Complainant further alleges that many residents lost their lives while those who survived were tortured by government forces.

The Complainant also alleges that in the use of what it considers to be excessive force to flush out the SLDF, the security forces set up by the Respondent State committed human rights violations and atrocities including indiscriminate burning of houses and food storage facilities and the killing of innocent people. Some of these deaths are allegedly attributed to the SLDF. The security forces of the Respondent State are also alleged to have engaged in indiscriminate arrests of residents without any information on the reasons for the arrests. They were also responsible for the beating of innocent people in a bid to extract information on the activities of the SLDF. The Complainant also alleges that the security forces engaged in extortion of money from residents to procure the release of those arrested.

The Complainant alleges that residents of Mount Elgon were subjected to sexual violence and other forms of torture. They were forced to whip each other, subjected to food and sleep deprivation and had their arms and limbs broken. They were also submerged in sewage, hanged upside down from a moving helicopter, forced to crawl on razor wire and forced to swallow sand. The Complainant alleges that civilians were the principal targets of these violations both by the forces of the Respondent State and the SLDF. In relation to violations that allegedly occurred on 15 and 16 December 2007, some of the Victims allegedly lost cash, livestock and household goods.

The Complainant claims that the Respondent State has no statistics on these events but that in conjunction with the Independent Medico-Legal Unit (IMLU), the Complainant has been able to get statements from residents on these violations. The Complaint further alleges that the Respondent State has failed to properly investigate these violations and that a report documented by the Kenyan National Commission on Human Rights on these violations has not resulted in the arrest or prosecution of anyone.
The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State has violated the rights of the residents of Mount Elgon as guaranteed in Articles 5, 6, 7 and 23 of the African Charter.

On 11 May 2010, the Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received the Complaint which was dated 30 April 2010. By letter dated 21 May 2010 the Secretariat informed the Complainant that the Complaint had been registered as Communication 385/10 1CJ Kenya v Kenya and slated for consideration by the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission) at its 47 Ordinary Session.

On 23 June 2010, the Secretariat wrote to both Parties to inform them that the Commission had considered the Complaint at its 47 Ordinary Session and had decided to be seized of it. The Secretariat also requested the Complainant to forward its Submissions on Admissibility in accordance with the Rules of Procedure.

Between 30 September 2010 and 26 May 2011, the Secretariat exchanged correspondence with the Parties concerning the submission of their respective arguments on the Admissibility of the Communication. On 14 July 2011, the Complainant's Submissions on Admissibility were received at the Secretariat and duly transmitted to the Respondent State.

On 11 November 2011 the Respondent State's Observations on the Admissibility of the Communication were received by the Secretariat at the 50 Ordinary Session of the Commission. On 19 June 2012, another copy of the Respondent State's Observations on the Admissibility of the Communication were received by the Secretariat as an email attachment.

In accordance with the Rules of Procedure of the Commission, a copy of the Respondent State's Observations on Admissibility was transmitted to the Complainant on 16 July 2012 along with a request to submit any comments thereto within one month.

Between 26 November 2012 and December 2012, the Secretariat exchanged correspondence with the Complainant regarding the Complainant's request for extension of time within which to submit its comments on the Respondent State's Observations on Admissibility.
On 18 January 2013, the Secretariat informed the Parties of the Commission's decision to grant the Complainant's request for an oral hearing at the 53 Ordinary Session of the Commission.

During its 53 Ordinary Session, the Commission heard the oral presentation of the Parties, admitted the Complainant's comments on the Respondent State's | Observations on Admissibility and deferred the consideration of the Communication.

At its 54 Ordinary Session held from 22 October to 5 November 2013, the Commission decided to defer consideration of the Communication due to time constraints. On 11 November 2013, the Secretariat informed both parties via a Note Verbale and letter notifying them of the Commission's decision.

During its 15 Extra-Ordinary Session held from 7 to 14 March 2014, the Commission considered the Admissibility of the Communication and decided to declare it admissible. The Parties were informed of the decision on 26 March 2014.

The decision on the Merits of the Communication was deferred during the 55 Ordinary Session of the Commission, pending submissions on the Merits from the Complainant and both Parties were duly informed on 29 May 2014.

The Complainant submitted on the Merits of the Communication on 17 June 2014. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt of the submissions and forwarded the same to the Respondent State on the same date, with an indication of the timeline for the State's observations on the Merits, that is, sixty (60) days, in line with Rule 108(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

On 11 March 2015, the Secretariat informed both Parties that the decision on the Merits was again deferred at the Commission's 17 Extra-Ordinary Session which took place from 19 to 28 February 2015, in Banjul, The Gambia, pending the State's submissions on the Merits, and that 30 Calendar Days had been granted to the State to make its submissions on the Merits to enable the Commission proceed with a decision on the Merits of the Communication at its next Session.
Up to the time of handing down this decision, the Respondent State had not submitted on the Merits, despite reminders to that effect. |
The Complainant submits that the Communication satisfies all the requirements for Admissibility as set out in Article 56 of the African Charter and should be declared admissible.

In relation to Article 56(1) of the African Charter, the Complainant submits that the violations alleged in the Communication are serious, massive and systemic. In such cases, the Complainant argues, there is no requirement to seek permission from the Victims before a Complaint is filed. The Complainant argues further that where a Complaint is in the supreme interest of the people of a state, there is no requirement that the consent of the Victim be sought before a Complaint is filed.

With reference to Article 56(2) of the African Charter, the Complainant submits that the Communication is in line with the objectives of the African Union (AU) and alleges violations of provisions of the African Charter.

The Complainant argues further in relation to Article 56(4) of the African Charter that the information relied upon in the Communication was obtained from a number of sources including direct interviews with Victims, documented investigations, and reports prepared by well founded, reliable and attested sources such as the Kenyan National Commission on Human Rights and the United Nations (UN) Special Rapporteur on Extra-Judicial Killings.

In relation to Article 56 (5) of the African Charter, the Complainant submits that the requirement to exhaust local remedies does not apply where the alleged violations have occurred on a large scale. The Complainant argues further that in such cases, the violations are well documented nationally and internationally over a period of time such that the State already has sufficient opportunity to remedy any wrongs.

Citing the jurisprudence of the Commission, the Complainant submits that in cases where there are many victims, as alleged in the present Communication, it is neither practicable nor desirable for victims to pursue internal remedies because the process will be unduly prolonged. The Complainant contends further that where the only effective remedy would be criminal investigation, prosecution and punishment of the perpetrators, and the Victims have done what is necessary to initiate proceedings, the requirement to exhaust local remedies is satisfied. This, the Complainant submits, applies to this Communication because reports were made to agencies of the Respondent State yet no action was taken.

The Complainant also submits that the Kenyan Police investigated the allegations in this Communication and submitted a report which the Respondent State relied upon while responding to enquiries made by the UN Committee Against Torture (CAT) in reaching its concluding observations. The Complainant submits that the Police report focused on land conflicts and did not address the complaints alleged in the present Communication.

The Complainant submits that the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights also conducted its independent investigations and made specific recommendations that touched on the issue of torture. However, the recommendations made by the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights in its report on the alleged violations were never implemented by the Respondent State.

The Complainant argues further that with specific reference to torture, enforced disappearances and witness protection, there are no domestic remedies as the Respondent State itself acknowledged in a report to the CAT that torture and other cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment or punishment are not defined by any national law.

Further, the Complainant submits that the majority of the residents whose relatives were actual Victims still retain fear of the Respondent State's security forces such that they cannot report violations to those same forces. The Complainant concludes that the Communication falls under the exception applicable to serious and massive violations and should therefore be considered to have satisfied the requirement to exhaust local remedies.

In relation to Article 56(6) of the African Charter, the Complainant argues that there has been no unreasonable delay in submitting the Communication. The Complainant submits that although the events complained of occurred between 2002 and 2008, the Kenyan Police began and carried out investigations for nearly two years. Thus, the Complainant had to await the outcome and implementation of the investigation before coming to the Commission. It was the failure to prosecute perpetrators after two years of the submission of various reports to the Respondent State that has warranted the submission of this Communication. The Complainant therefore concludes that the Communication satisfies the requirements of Article 56(6) of the Charter.

Regarding the requirement in Article 56(7) of the African Charter, the Complainant submits that the Communication has not been brought and is not currently before any other international body. The Complainant therefore urges the Commission to declare the Communication admissible.

In its Observations on Admissibility, the Respondent State contends that the Communication is not admissible because it does not satisfy some of the requirements set out in Article 56 of the African Charter.

With regard to Article 56(1) of the African Charter, the Respondent State submits that there is no relationship between the Complainant and the alleged Victims. The Respondent State submits further that no list of alleged Victims has been attached to confirm that the Complainant has authority to act on behalf of the alleged Victims.

The Respondent State argues further that the Communication ought to have been submitted in the name of the Victims. Where personal submission by the Victim is not possible, the Respondent State argues that the Victim ought to authorise the submission of a Complaint but no such authority is shown by the Complainant. The Respondent State contends further that the Complainant has not demonstrated it has the locus standi to lodge the Communication, or that it has been instructed by specifically named individuals who are Victims of the alleged violations. The Respondent State also submits that for failing to mention and identify the alleged Victims of the violations in the Communication, the Complainant has not satisfied Article 56(1) of the African Charter.

With regard to Article 56(5) of the African Charter, the Respondent State contends that local remedies have not been exhausted and that the exception applicable in cases of massive violations is not a general rule and it does not apply to this Communication. The Respondent State submits that the alleged violations in this Communication, if any, are not "widespread and out of control" but only restricted to an area covering Mount Elgon District where threats have currently been eliminated.

The Respondent State submits further that local remedies exist within its legal system which the Complainant should have exhausted before bringing the Communication to the Commission. In this regard, the Respondent State submits that the Complainant should have filed a constitutional reference to the High Court of Kenya in accordance with Section 84(1) of the Kenyan Constitution since that court has constitutional powers to hear, determine and redress breaches of human rights. The Respondent State adds that as stated in its national jurisprudence, the right of access to the Kenyan High Court is expansive and the Complainant could have approached the High Court for redress on the facts.

Regarding the legislative framework for the protection of the affected rights, the Respondent State submits that the "right to life, the right to property and the right to freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment" are recognised and protected by the Kenyan Constitution. The Respondent State argues therefore that Kenyan courts have an obligation to protect rights and several courts have done so.

The Respondent State submits further that apart from judicial remedies, a number of quasi-judicial remedies are available within the Kenyan legal system which the Complainant should have first exhausted. The Respondent State lists the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights, the Truth, Justice and Reconciliation Commission, the National Cohesion and Integration Commission and the Kenya National Land Commission as other bodies that should have been exhausted by the Complainant.

The Respondent State adds that the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights visited the Mount Elgon District area, carried out investigations and published a report with recommendations which the government is implementing. The Respondent State contends that the remedies it has listed are capable of redressing the Complaint and it is incumbent on the Complainant to, at least, attempt those remedies before coming to the Commission. The Respondent State concludes that the Complainant has failed to exhaust local remedies in relation to the Communication.

Regarding Article 56(6) of the African Charter, the Respondent State submits that the government is still dealing with the issues within the Mount Elgon District. The Respondent State contends that this means that local remedies have not been exhausted and the Complainant ought to bring the Complaint within a reasonable time from the time local remedies are exhausted.

In relation to Article 56(7) of the African Charter, the Respondent State submits that the root cause of the dispute was "land allocation gone awry" and that that issue has been resolved. Thus, the Respondent State argues that the matter has been resolved and dealing with the Communication will "reopen the underlying issues" and complicate or hinder the resolution of those issues. The Respondent State submits further that the issues sought to be addressed by the Communication have also received the attention of the UN High Commissioner on Human Rights. The report of the High Commissioner containing specific recommendations was received by the Government and is currently being implemented.

The Respondent State submits further that the issues in the Communication have also received the attention of the East African Court of Justice (EACJ). The case before the EACJ was filed on 2 July 2010 by IMLU, a Non-Governmental Organisation based in Kenya. The Respondent State concludes that the issues in the Communication have been considered or are being considered by other competent institutions and that the implementation of recommendations on aspects of the Communication makes it moot. The Respondent State concludes that the Communication has not satisfied some of the requirements in Article 56 of the African Charter and should be declared inadmissible.

In response to the Respondent State's observations, the Complainant submits that in spite of the Respondent State's argument that the Communication relates to land allocation in the Mount Elgon area, the land conflict is not the subject of its interest. The Complainant avers that the Communication is concerned with the incidents of torture, summary and extra-judicial executions, disappearances and other forms of cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment allegedly meted out to over 4000 civilians by agents of the Respondent State and other non-state actors. The Complainant argues that the issues are therefore not moot issues as claimed by the Respondent State.

Regarding the Respondent State's observations on Article 56(1) of the African Charter, the Complainant responds that both the letter of the Charter and the jurisprudence of the Commission indicate that all that is required is for the names of the authors to be indicated on the Complaint and not necessarily the names of the Victims. On this point, the Complainant refers the Commission to Bakweri Land Claims Committee v Cameroon, Gunme et al v Cameroon and Malawi African Association and Others v Mauritania.

The Complainant submits further that the African Charter does not contain any Victim requirement nor does it require prior authorisation by Victims before a Communication is brought. The Complainant argues that it has therefore satisfied Article 56(1) of the African Charter.

In reaction to the Respondent State's observation on Article 56(5) of the African Charter, the Complainant contends that some of the remedies identified by the Respondent State were not available at the time the events occurred. Accordingly, the Complainant argues further, it could not have been expected to exhaust those non-existent remedies. The Complainant argues that the High Court Constitutional review procedure under Section 84(1) of the Kenyan Constitution suggested by the Respondent State only came into existence under the 2010 Kenyan Constitution, some two years after the events.

The Complainant argues that the Section 84(1) provision that was available under the previous Kenyan Constitution was only available to an individual on his own behalf or on behalf of some other person in detention. Arguing that the previous Section 84(1) gave no option to enforce rights in the public interest, it would have meant that in each case an applicant would have had to demonstrate a personal interest in the matter before a Kenyan High Court. The Complainant contends that exhausting the constitutional reference remedy would therefore have required every single Victim to approach the court individually and this was impractical.

While conceding that the Kenyan Police carried out investigations into the matter, the Complainant submits that the Police investigations did not address the issues of torture as it should have. The Complainant submits that recommendations in other reports by the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights, the Kenya Peace and Reconciliation Commission and the UN Special Rapporteur on Extra-Judicial, Summary or Arbitrary Executions as well as concluding observations of the United Nations Committee Against Torture were also not implemented by the Respondent State.

The Complainant submits further that even assuming the Victims could approach the Kenyan courts, that fact alone could not provide redress for the core of the Complaint. This, according to the Complainant, is because the Communication relates to the failure of the Respondent State to exercise due diligence to prevent the violation and the failure to investigate, prosecute and punish the perpetrators. The Complainant argues that post facto civil remedies including constitutional references do not lead to the prosecution of perpetrators and are therefore an insufficient remedy in the circumstances.

Reacting to the Respondent State's contention that the alleged violations are neither massive nor serious, the Complainant submits that the violations were both massive and serious as all peoples in the area of Mount Elgon were affected. Citing reports by Human Rights Watch and figures allegedly released by the Kenyan Military, the Complainant avers that at least seventy-two (72) people died; thirty four (34) people were missing while thousands were detained. The Complainant further cites a report by the Kenyan National Commission on Human Rights which stated that between 66, 000 and 200,000 people were displaced as at April 2008. These statistics, the Complainant submits, indicate the serious and massive nature of the alleged violations.

The Complainant in summary urges the Commission to find that local remedies were either not available or if available, were insufficient and could not have been exhausted. The Complainant argues further that the exceptions to the requirement to exhaust local remedies apply because of the massive and serious nature of the alleged violations.

Regarding the Respondent State's observation on Article 56(6) of the African Charter, the Complainant contends that the requirement to submit within a reasonable time does not apply where the exception to the exhaustion of local remedies rule is invoked. Citing Interights (on behalf of Pan African Movement and Citizens for Peace in Eritrea) v Eritrea and Ethiopia, the Complainant argues further that the reasonable time requirement is rendered inapplicable where it is found that no domestic remedies were available to the Victims. The Complainant contends that the present circumstances warrant the suspension of the requirement in Article 56(6) of the African Charter in relation to the present Communication.

Concerning the Respondent State's observation on Article 56(7) of the African Charter, the Complainant submits that the settlement of the land allocation issue is different from the issues raised in the present Communication. The Complainant argues further that it is not a party to the case before the EACJ and that that case has no bearing on the present Communication. The Complainant submits further that the EACJ does not have a human rights jurisdiction and proceedings before that court cannot be covered by Article 56(7) of the African Charter. Citing Bob Njoku v Egypt, the Complainant sums up that as far as a decision on the merits has not been reached, the Communication meets the requirement in Article 56(7) of the Charter.

The Communication is brought under Article 55 of the African Charter dealing with Communications other than Inter-State Communications therefore it needs to satisfy the seven conditions for Admissibility set out in Article 56 of the Charter. The Commission notes that the Respondent State has not challenged the Complainant's claims and arguments concerning the requirements in Article 56 (2) (3) and (4) of the African Charter.

The Commission's own assessment of the Communication indicates that the conditions in Article 56(2), (3) and (4) of the African Charter are satisfied. The Commission particularly notes that it can only consider Communications that 'are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or to the Organisation of African Unity. The Commission does not find such insulting or disparaging language in the Communication. Consequently, the Commission's analysis will focus on the requirements set out in Article 56(1), (5) (6) and (7) of the Charter.

Article 56(1) of the African Charter provides that Communications submitted to the Commission should 'indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity'. The Complainant argues that it has satisfied this requirement since the provision does not require it to show that it has the consent or authority of the Victims especially where the alleged violation is of a serious and massive nature as is the case in the present Communication.

The Respondent State disputes the Complainant's claim regarding Article 56(1) of the African Charter and instead argues that the Complainant has not satisfied the requirement since it has not shown that it has any relationship with the Victims of the alleged violations and has not attached any list of the alleged Victims in order to confirm that it has the authority to act on their behalf.

The Respondent State argues further that Article 56(1) of the Charter requires the Communication to have been submitted in the name of the Victims but the Complainant has failed to do so. The Respondent State also submits that the alleged Victims ought to have authorised the submission of the Communication and in the absence of such authority, the Complainant has failed to demonstrate that it has the locus standi to lodge the Communication. The Respondent State contends therefore that the Complainant's failure to mention and identify the alleged Victims amounts to a failure to satisfy the requirement in Article 56(1) of the African Charter.

The Commission notes that Article 56(1) of the Charter requires that a Communication should not be submitted anonymously. As this Commission has noted in its earlier decision in Malawi African Association v Mauritania, Article 56(1) of the Charter demands that any person submitting a Communication to the Commission must reveal his or her identity. It does not necessarily require that the author(s) of the Communication must be the Victims of the alleged violation or members of the family of the alleged Victims.

In Gunme et al v Cameroon, this Commission reaffirmed that Article 56(1) of the African Charter only requires a Communication to indicate its authors and not necessarily the Victims of the violations alleged in the Communication. The Commission also recalls that it has previously held that it adopts a liberal approach to locus standi under the African Charter. Accordingly, in submitting a Communication alleging a violation of rights guaranteed in the Charter, the author need not be the Victim or a member of the Victim's family. The author of a Communication does not also need any special authority to act on behalf of the Victim and does not need to show any particular interest in order to qualify to submit the Communication. The Commission therefore finds that the Communication satisfies the requirement in Article 56(1) of the African Charter.

Article 56(5) of the African Charter requires that Communications 'are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged'. The Complainant contends that the Communication satisfies Article 56(5) of the African Charter even though no attempt was made to exhaust local remedies. The Complainant submits that the requirement to exhaust local remedies does not apply where the alleged violations have occurred on a large scale. The Complainant cites earlier jurisprudence of the Commission and argues that where there are many Victims of the violation alleged in a Communication, it is neither practicable nor desirable to pursue local remedies as the process will be unduly prolonged.

The Complainant argues in addition that the nature of relief sought in the Communication cannot be provided by a civil action before the national courts since those proceedings do not result in the investigation, prosecution and punishment of perpetrators of human rights violations. It is also the Complainant's argument that the local remedies identified by the Respondent State in its observations were either not available at the relevant time for it to be exhausted or would not have been sufficient to redress the alleged violation. The Complainant therefore contends that the exceptions to the requirement to exhaust local remedies apply to the present Communication.

The Respondent State concedes that an exception to the requirement to exhaust local remedies is applicable in cases of serious and massive violations of human rights. However, the Respondent State contends that the exception is not a general rule and does not apply to the present Communication because the violations alleged are not widespread or out of control but are restricted to an area covering the Mount Elgon District.

The Commission recalls its earlier jurisprudence that in situations involving serious and massive violations of human rights, it is impracticable and undesirable to require the Complainant to exhaust local remedies before coming before the Commission. However, the Commission notes that while the Parties agree on the applicable legal principle, there is a dispute of fact regarding the question whether the present Communication involves serious and massive violations such that the exception to Article 56(5) should apply.

Although the Commission has not prescribed the criteria for determining what constitutes serious and massive violations of human rights under the African Charter, the existing jurisprudence of the Commission provides sufficient guidance for making such a determination. As represented in the Commission's decision in Sudan Human Rights Organisation & Another v Sudan, this Commission considers both the scale and nature of the alleged violations in determining whether the violations are serious and massive.

In terms of the scale, the Commission believes that violations are massive where a significant number of people are targeted either within a specific area or across the territory of a State Party. In terms of the nature, the Commission considers violations to be massive where they are the product of a consistent and predetermined action that impacts on a right or a combination of rights guaranteed under the African Charter.

In the present Communication, the Commission notes that over three thousand (3000) persons are alleged to have been directly targeted while another group comprising of tens of thousands of people was allegedly displaced. The Commission notes further that a number of rights some of which touch on the dignity of the human being are affected. The Commission believes that this constitutes a prima facie case of serious and massive violations. In such situations, as this Commission has previously observed, it is both impracticable and undesirable to require the Complainant to exhaust local remedies.

The Commission further recalls its jurisprudence that only local remedies that are available, effective and sufficient are required to be exhausted by a Complainant coming before the African Commission. As this Commission has also previously held, where a Complainant contends that it has not exhausted local remedies because they do not exist and the Respondent State argues otherwise, the onus to prove their existence lies on the Respondent State. The Respondent State has not established satisfactorily how the local remedies that it identified could have been effective and sufficient in the particular circumstances of the violations alleged in this Communication.

The Commission also recalls that the reference to local remedies in the African Charter relates to judicial remedies or remedies of a judicial nature that hold the promise of a binding obligation of enforcement by a State Party. The non-judicial remedies that the Respondent State has listed such as the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights and the Kenya Truth and Reconciliation Commission do not have that judicial character and need not be exhausted by the Complainant. In the absence of effective and sufficient local remedies, the Commission finds that the exceptions to the requirement to exhaust local remedies apply to the Communication.

In relation to the requirement in Article 56(6) of the African Charter, the Complainant submits that it was after the failure of the Respondent State to implement the recommendations that it took the decision to come before the Commission. The Complainant argues further that in any case, in the absence of local remedies, the requirement to submit a Complaint within a reasonable time after exhaustion of local remedies does not apply to the present Communication.

The Respondent State argues that the Complainant has not exhausted local remedies therefore time should not start to run as envisaged in Article 56(6) of the African Charter. In other words, the Respondent State takes the view that time does not start to run until local remedies are exhausted. It is therefore the Respondent State's position that the Communication is not even ripe for submission.

Article 56(6) of the African Charter provides that Communications shall be considered if they 'are submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized with the matter'. As the Commission has noted in its jurisprudence, the African Charter does not define what constitutes a reasonable period of time. Accordingly, even in cases where local remedies are required to be exhausted and are exhausted, the Commission considers each case on its own merit in determining what constitutes a reasonable period of time.

The Commission is of the opinion that in situations where it is undesirable or impracticable for Victims to exhaust local remedies because such remedies are unavailable, ineffective or insufficient or are unduly prolonged, the submission of a Complaint is no longer tied to the exhaustion of local remedies. Accordingly, the Commission does not agree with the Respondent State's view that the Complainant cannot bring the Communication until local remedies are exhausted.

The Commission notes the Complainant's submission that the alleged violations occurred between 2002 and 2008 but the Communication was filed in 2010 because the results of several investigations were being awaited. The Commission also notes the Complainant's claim that it had to give the national authorities time to try to implement the recommendations that followed those investigations. The Commission is aware that in certain situations involving serious and massive violations, the challenges involved in entering the area and collecting required evidence may be higher than usual.

The Commission also notes that the Complainant did not stay idle during this period but explored other avenues to trigger the implementation of the recommendations that it considered relevant for redressing the alleged violations. In the particular circumstance of this Communication, considering the nature of government business at the national level and the difficulties associated with processing complaints involving serious and massive violations, the Commission believes that the Complainant has not unreasonably delayed in submitting the Communication. The Commission therefore finds that Article 56(6) of the African Charter has been satisfied.

Regarding Article 56(7) of the African Charter, the Respondent State contends that the Communication falls foul of this Article because the root cause of the dispute was land allocation which has been resolved. It states that dealing with the Communication will "re-open the underlying issues" and complicate or hinder the resolution of those issues. The State further argues that the matter received the attention of the EACJ, in a case filed by the IMLU on 2 July 2010. In rebuttal, the Complainant submits that the settlement of the land allocation issue is different from the issues raised in the present Communication; it is not a party to the case before the EACJ and that the case before the EACJ has no bearing on the present Communication. The Complainant also alludes to recommendations made by the UN Special Rapporteur on Extra-Judicial, Summary or Arbitrary Executions which have also not been implemented by the Respondent State.

The Commission also notes that some of the issues in the Communication were brought to the attention of the CAT, a fact which was not addressed by either Party in their submissions under Article 56(7) of the African Charter.

Article 56(7) of the African Charter provides that Communications before the Commission shall only be considered if they "do not deal with cases which have been settled by those States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the present Charter." In Gunme et al v Cameroon, this Commission noted that Article 56(7) of the African Charter bars the Commission from entertaining cases that have been settled by another international settlement procedure, and the Treaty or Charter body dealing with the matter should have taken a decision which addresses the concerns, including the relief being sought by the Complainant.

The import of the requirement under Article 56(7) is therefore, that the matter in contention, which must relate to the same facts and parties, must have been "settled" - it must no longer be under consideration under an international dispute-settlement procedure. Also, the prior settlement of the matter must have been by a body "capable of granting declaratory or compensatory relief to victims, not mere political resolutions and declarations" that is, "an international adjudication mechanism, with a human rights mandate".

At this point, it is imperative for the Commission to ascertain whether the matter before the EACJ and the CAT has been 'settled' or not. The immediate question to be answered is whether the EACJ and the CAT are bodies envisaged under Article 56(7).

The EACJ is a Regional Court with a human rights mandate, while the CAT is a UN Treaty Body-created under international human rights treaties, with a complaint handling mechanism. In this regard, the EACJ and the CAT fall within the purview of Article 56(7) of the African Charter. Having established this, can we say for a fact that these bodies 'settled' the matter currently before the Commission?

Regarding the EACJ, the Commission notes that the Respondent State has not indicated that the present Complainant is involved in the case before the EACJ- it only made reference to the IMLU. The State has also not demonstrated that the case before the EACJ involves the same human rights issues as presented in this Communication, nor indicated that the case before the EACJ has been settled on its merits as envisaged by Article 56(7) of the African Charter. This notwithstanding, the Commission agrees with the Complainant that it is not a party to the matter before the EACJ, and without any evidence from the Respondent State to state otherwise, the subject matter of the present Communication is not the same subject matter before the EACJ which already eliminates some of the conditions for establishing that a matter has been 'settled'. Additionally, the matter resolved by the Respondent State is the issue of allocation of land which is not the subject matter of this Communication and which has no bearing on the same.

On the recommendations made by the UN Special Rapporteur on Extra-Judicial, Summary or Arbitrary Executions, firstly, the latter is not a Treaty or Charter Body as contemplated under Article 56(7) of the Charter. Secondly, the Commission has averred that settlement of the matter must have been by a body "capable of granting declaratory or compensatory relief to victims...." The recommendations by the UN Special Rapporteur on Extra-Judicial, Summary or Arbitrary Executions do not fall within this context.

With respect to the CAT, the Commission notes that the matter in this Communication was brought to the attention of the CAT through a State Report by the Respondent State during CAT's 41 Session from 3 to 21 November 2008, and Concluding Observations were made therefrom. There was no Complaint brought before the CAT, and no adjudication process per se. The recommendations referenced by the Complainant, and which have allegedly not been implemented by the Respondent State are recommendations made by the CAT following consideration of the State Report. Accordingly, the Commission finds that the Communication satisfies the condition in Article 56(7) of the African Charter because the subject matter of the Communication has not been 'settled' as anticipated by Article 56(7) of the African Charter.
In view of the above, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares this Communication Admissible.

The Complainant alleges that the conflict in Mt Elgon started in 2006 through to 2008 when the people of Mt Elgon were attacked repeatedly by a rebel group, the Sabaot Land Defence Force (SLDF). The attacks continued in 2008 when the State sent in a security operation aimed at bringing peace, but instead launched more terror on the civilians. According to the Complainant, civilians were the principle targets for murder, abduction, forced recruitment and displacement as both militia groups and the army besieged villages abducting, re-abducting, and arresting civilians and committing atrocities and indiscriminate killings.

The Complainant submits that the Victims were subjected to massive and systematic violations of human rights. They were arbitrarily arrested by the army, detained, tortured and robbed then released without charges. The Complainant states that the Victims were principal targets of murder, abduction, forced recruitment and forced displacement in the conflict that ensued between the State and State security agents.

It also alleges that the Victims have been denied a remedy to the violations as there are no current government statistics that reflect the number of those displaced, dead, or even actual residents of this region and that although the cases were reported there were no investigations by the Respondent State, and even where investigations were carried out there has neither been prosecution nor willingness to arrest the perpetrators of the violence.

The Complainant submits that this conduct violated articles 5, 6, 7 and 23 of the African Charter. The Commission notes that in its Complaint the Complainant alleges violations of Articles 5, 6, 7 and 23 (1) of the Charter. However substantially its merits arguments address Articles 5 and 6. Substantially, the Commission will draw arguments from the initial Complaint to buttress allegations of violations of Articles 7 and 23(1).

The Complainant submits that the Commission should find the Respondent State in violation of articles 5, 6, 7 and 23, of the Charter and direct the government of Kenya: a) To invite the Commission to establish an independent investigations mechanism to effectively go into Kenya and in Mount Elgon to conduct an extensive investigation of the alleged violations; b) To provide adequate and efficiently coordinated security personnel in all parts of Mount Elgon; c) To immediately, diligently, genuinely and effectively investigate and prosecute SLDF and state security agents, soldiers and any other persons who violated the rights of citizens in Mt Elgon and serve the Commission with a progress report; d) To establish an independent agency to conduct thorough investigations, set recommendations for those to be prosecuted immediately, in respect of civilians whose rights have been violated. A progress report should be lodged with the Commission at reasonable intervals; e) To declare that the recruitment of militia groups amounts to a violation of the Charter for which the government of Kenya is responsible; f) To adopt measures such as provision of psychosocial care facilities for the rehabilitation of all civilians affected by the violence and other historical injustices in Mount Elgon including militias.

The Complainant also urges the Commission to carry out a fact-finding Mission to Kenya in order to come up with a lasting solution to the predicament of the people of Mount Elgon pursuant to the provisions of Article 45(1) whereby the Commission may "use any appropriate method of investigating any matter falling within the ambit of the present Charter".

The Commission is called upon to determine whether the Respondent State, in allegedly failing to ensure the security of the people of Mount Elgon, targeting them for murder, abduction, forced recruitment and displacement, and failure to prevent militia groups from besieging villages abducting, re-abducting civilians and committing atrocities and indiscriminate killings, and to investigate such attacks, violated provisions of the African Charter.

The Commission notes from the onset that the Respondent State did not make any observations on the Complainant's submissions on the Merits despite several reminders to that effect. In the absence of specific observations on the Merits from the Respondent State, the Commission has relied on the Complainant's submissions on the Merits, as well as the Respondent State's submissions on Admissibility which addressed aspects of the Merits of this Communication.

The Complainant attributes several acts to the Respondent State perpetrated against the Victims and argues that these acts amounted to torture in violation of Article 5 of the African Charter. These acts include sustained beatings with sticks and army boots, stripping naked and beating people while naked, frog-marching and forcing people to roll on the ground while being beaten.

The Complainant points out that the right to freedom from torture is absolutely prohibited and protected under the African Charter. The Complainant refers to the Commission's decision in Communications 137/94, 139/94, 154/96 and 161/97- International Pen, Constitutional Rights Project, Interights on behalf of Ken Saro Wiwa v Nigeria wherein the Commission found torture to include: Actions which cause serious physical or psychological suffering or humiliate the individual or force him or her to act against his or her will or conscience.

The Complainant explains that the methods of torture used by the Respondent State's security forces caused serious injuries and even though the cases were reported, there have been no state investigations, prosecution nor willingness to arrest the perpetrators of the violence.

Further, the Complainant avers that in failing to collect or possess data and records of these violations, the Government of Kenya has shown lack of due diligence to prevent violations especially those committed by its officers and contends that this constitutes a violation of Article 5 of the Charter.

The Complainant contends that the State failed to exercise its duty to protect civilians from various conduct and vices detrimental to the enjoyment of their rights as was articulated by the Commission in Social and Economic Rights Action Centre (SERAC) and the Center for Economic and Social Rights v Nigeria.
