This rectification, the Complainant explains, was based on the erroneous nature of the first results. Referring to the erroneous results, the Complainant thus reports that, although the elections were combined, the number of voters had increased excessively while the number of polling stations compiled had decreased. Concerning the constituency of Mbujimayi Ville where he was elected, the Complainant indicates, for example, that the number of voters was 279,763 for the presidential election (count from 807 polling stations) as against 307,417 for the legislative election (count from 748 polling stations).

The Complainant states that, in response to the petition contesting the results submitted by the other candidate, the Supreme Court reinstated the erroneous results by delivering the judgment of 25 April 2012 by which it invalidated his mandate and replaced him with the author of the said petition. The Court is said to have done so even though the witnesses had mentioned serious errors in the minutes and consequently refused to sign them, thereby rendering null the first results posted, as provided for in Article 56 of the Implementing Measures of Electoral Law No. 11/003 of 25 June 2011. Furthermore, the Complainant reports that, under the provisions of Article 75 of the Electoral Law relating to the procedure for handling petitions contesting results, the Supreme Court had no power to replace a candidate but should rather have referred the file back to the CENI for a recount of the votes or the organisation of a new ballot.

In reaction to the judgment invalidating his mandate, the Complainant submitted two applications for rectification of material errors on 03 May and 25 June 2012 respectively. By a judgment of 05 September 2012, the Supreme Court declared the said applications inadmissible. Furthermore, having been seized of the petition contesting the results on 7 February 2012, the Supreme Court ruled on it only on 25 April 2012, whereas the law imposed on it a time limit of two months at most.

As soon as the first decision of 25 June 2012 was delivered and without waiting for the disputes concerning the two applications for rectification of errors to be disposed of, the National Assembly suspended the Complainant's installation allowances and remuneration. Furthermore, the parliamentary institution proceeded, on 04 May 2012, to install the candidate declared elected by the Supreme Court in place of the Complainant.

Finally, the Complainant states that, having been seized by all the members of parliament who suffered the same fate, the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) dispatched a mission of its Committee on the Human Rights of Parliamentarians which stayed in the DRC from 26 July to 1 August 2012. Basing itself on the Report of the said mission, which had concluded that Congolese electoral law and human rights had been violated by the institutions involved in the process, the IPU had, on 24 October 2012, adopted a Resolution calling on the DRC authorities to remedy the situation.
The Complainant alleges the violation of the rights guaranteed by Articles 3, 7, 13 and 15 of the African Charter.

He prays the Commission to request the Democratic Republic of the Congo to: - Redress the alleged violations by his reinstatement in the National Assembly; - Compensate him for the harm caused, with all the other benefits of the office, including parliamentary immunities; - Ratify the Protocol establishing the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights and make the declaration provided for in Article 34(6) of the said Protocol.

The Complaint reached the Secretariat on 13 December 2012. On 18 December 2012, the Secretariat acknowledged receipt of it and informed the Complainant that it would be considered at the 13 Extraordinary Session of the Commission scheduled to be held from 18 to 25 February 2013 in Banjul, The Gambia.

At its 13 Extraordinary Session, the Commission considered the Complaint and decided to be seized of it. On 1 March 2013, the Secretariat informed the Parties of this decision and requested the Complainant to submit his observations on Admissibility. The said observations were received on 08 March 2013. On 11 March 2013, the Secretariat acknowledged receipt of them and transmitted them to the Respondent State.

At its 53 Ordinary Session held from 09 to 23 April 2013 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Communication and decided to defer its decision for failure to submit the Respondent State's brief. On 03 May 2013, the Parties were informed of this decision and a reminder was sent to the Respondent State.

On 1 July 2013, the Complainant seized the Commission with a request for provisional measures. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 2 July 2013 and indicated to the Complainant that his request would be submitted to the Commission at the next session.

At its 14 Extraordinary Session held from 20 to 24 July in Nairobi, Kenya, the Commission considered the Communication and decided to defer it again, owing to time constraints. The Parties were informed thereof on 13 August 2013.

At its 54 Ordinary Session held from 22 October to 5 November 2013 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Communication and deferred it for the preparation of a decision on the basis of the information in its possession, given that the Respondent State had not submitted its brief on Admissibility. The Parties were informed thereof on 12 November 2013. On 15 November 2013, the Secretariat also informed the Complainant that the Commission had considered his request for provisional measures and decided not to grant it.

At its successive sessions, the Commission considered the Communication and decided to defer it owing to time constraints. The Parties were duly informed thereof. At its 17 Extraordinary Session held from 19 to 28 February 2015 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Communication and declared it admissible. The Secretariat informed the Parties thereof and requested the Complainant to submit his observations on the merits.

On 17 March 2015, the Complainant transmitted his observations on the merits, which were transmitted to the Respondent State on 19 March 2015. As the Secretariat had not received the Respondent State's observations on the merits at the expiry of the time limit provided for in the Rules of Procedure, a final time limit of one month was granted to the State to do so. The related correspondence was transmitted on 8 June 2015. The Complainant was informed thereof. At its successive sessions, the Commission considered the Communication and deferred it for lack of time.

Relying on the observations he submitted for that purpose, the Complainant maintains that the Communication complies with all the admissibility requirements prescribed in Article 56 of the African Charter. Thus, the Complainant maintains that the requirement laid down in Article 56(1) is fulfilled since he is the author of the Communication and has not requested anonymity. He also maintains that the Communication complies with Article 56(2) because it falls within the scope ratione materiae and ratione temporis of the African Charter and of the Constitutive Act of the African Union, because it alleges violations of provisions of the Charter, and finally, because it is submitted against a State Party to the said Charter by a Complainant of the nationality of that State.

Furthermore, to prove compliance with the requirement of Article 56(4), the Complainant indicates that his Complaint is made up of documents transmitted to the CENI, judgments of the Supreme Court and decisions of the IPU. As regards the exhaustion of local remedies required by Article 56(5), the Complainant alleges that the Communication complies with this requirement given that the Supreme Court, the last resort at the national level, considered the case and delivered a decision. Finally, the Complainant reports that he seized the IPU, which acknowledged the arbitrary nature of the invalidation of his mandate.

As the procedure clearly reflects, the Respondent State has not produced a defence brief, despite the fact that, between 11 March 2013 and 23 May 2014, the Secretariat sent it multiple correspondences to that end.

This Communication was submitted on the basis of Article 55 of the African Charter, which gives the Commission jurisdiction to receive and consider "communications other than those of States parties". To be declared admissible, such communications must meet the requirements laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter.

In accordance with the provisions of Rule 105(1) of its Rules of Procedure, when the Commission decides to be seized of a communication, it immediately transmits a copy to the Respondent State, informs the Complainant of its decision and invites him to present his arguments and evidence on Admissibility within two months. Furthermore, once the Complainant's arguments are received, the Secretariat transmits them to the Respondent State for a reply within two months of notification.

In this case, the Commission notes that the procedural requirements thus recalled were observed, as attested by the Notes Verbales reminding the Respondent State to transmit its observations on Admissibility. The Commission finds that the State did not respond to the said correspondence and therefore decides to examine the Communication on the basis of the elements in its possession, in accordance with its practice.

As the Respondent State has not produced a brief on Admissibility, the Commission will proceed to an examination of all the requirements laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter. Beginning with the requirement laid down in Article 56(1), the Commission notes that the Communication clearly identifies its author as Mr Albert Bialufu Ngandu, a Congolese national, whose full address is on file. Furthermore, the Complainant has remained constantly in communication with the Secretariat and has undertaken all the diligence required under the procedure. The Commission therefore considers that the Communication complies with the requirement examined.

With regard to compliance with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter, the Commission recalls that the requirement laid down is understood as the compatibility ratione personae, ratione materiae, ratione temporis and ratione loci of the Communication with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Charter. In plain terms, the examination of compatibility must consist, for the Commission, in ensuring that all the arguments and claims contained in the Communication are consistent with the provisions of the instruments cited above.

In this case, the Commission notes that the Communication is submitted against the DRC, a State Party to the African Charter, and that the Complainant has standing. Furthermore, the Complainant alleges the violation, on the territory of the Respondent State, of rights protected by the Charter, at a time when the latter was in force at the time of the facts. Finally, neither the arguments invoked nor the claims made are contrary to any of the principles contained in the African Charter and the Constitutive Act of the African Union. The Commission concludes that the Communication complied with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter.

As regards compliance with the provisions of Article 56(3), the Commission notes, in light of its jurisprudence, that the Communication contains no term that could be characterised as insulting or disparaging towards the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union. The Commission also notes that the requirement laid down in Article 56(4) is met since the Communication contains, among other things, official documents produced by the institutions of the Respondent State including the CENI and the Supreme Court as well as by the IPU.

On the exhaustion of local remedies required by Article 56(5) of the African Charter, the Commission notes that following the proclamation of his election by the CENI and his taking up office in the National Assembly, the Complainant saw his candidacy invalidated by a judgment of the Supreme Court dated 25 April 2012. The two applications submitted by the Complainant for rectification of the material errors contained in the first decision were declared inadmissible by another judgment of 05 September 2012.

The Commission notes that the Supreme Court of the DRC acts as Constitutional Court with jurisdiction in electoral matters. Furthermore, the decisions of the said court are not open to appeal. The applications for rectification submitted by the Complainant having been rejected, no further remedy was available to him in the settlement of the said dispute. The Commission concludes that local remedies have been exhausted.

With regard to compliance with the provisions of Article 56(6), the Commission notes that the decision of the Supreme Court amounting to the exhaustion of local remedies dates from 05 September 2012. The Complaint reached the Secretariat on 13 December 2012, that is, less than four months after the exhaustion of local remedies. In accordance with its jurisprudence, the Commission finds that this time frame for seizure is reasonable and that the requirement under examination is fulfilled.

Finally, under the provisions of Article 56(7), the Communication must not deal with cases which have been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the African Charter. The Commission recalls that these provisions require the Communication to respect the principles of res judicata; of non-lis pendens; and of non bis in idem.

In this case, the Commission notes that, apart from the actions undertaken before the national courts, the Complainant brought this matter before the Human Rights Committee of the Inter-Parliamentary Union, which adopted a Resolution calling on the DRC to take the necessary measures to remedy the Complainant's situation. While acknowledging the relevance and usefulness of the procedures undertaken by the IPU in the context of this case, the Commission refers to its jurisprudence cited supra, to recall the meaning of the requirement of res judicata laid down in Article 56(7) of the African Charter. In this regard, the Commission reiterates that decisions of the United Nations Treaty Bodies or of any other international bodies with a mandate to hear complaints concerning human rights violations may constitute res judicata, provided that the said bodies apply principles consistent with those prescribed in Article 56(7) of the African Charter.

The Commission notes that the Human Rights Committee of the IPU is not a United Nations treaty body, nor does it apply the principles set out in Article 56(7) of the African Charter. Furthermore, the case is not pending before any other body referred to in the provisions of the same Article. Finally, and consequently, there is no reason to fear that the Respondent State may be subjected to double prosecution, let alone a conviction in the same case. The Commission concludes that the Communication complies with the requirement examined.
In sum, the Commission finds that the Communication complies with all the requirements laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter and that it should therefore be declared admissible.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares this Communication admissible in accordance with the provisions of Article 56 of the Charter.
Whereas he initially alleges only the violation of Articles 3, 7, 13 and 15 of the Charter, the Complainant extends his claims to Articles 1 and 26 at the merits stage.
The Complainant maintains that the absence of a double degree of jurisdiction before the Supreme Court violates his right to equal protection of the law in comparison with other Congolese litigants.

The Complainant alleges the partiality of the courts, which he supports by the fact that the Supreme Court's judgments relied on erroneous documents and were not notified in full. He further alleges that the Court violated the right to a reasoned decision by delivering judgments on the basis of minutes disputed by the Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) and the witnesses. According to the Complainant, the time limits for justice were also not respected in that judgments were delivered beyond the time limits prescribed by law and were published only as to the operative part. As regards the principle of double degree of jurisdiction, the Complainant maintains that it was violated by the impossibility of appealing the decisions rendered by the Supreme Court.

According to the Complainant, the provisions of this Article of the Charter were violated in that the Court granted the capacity to sit as a member of parliament to a candidate who did not obtain the votes of the electors.
The Complainant maintains that, having been unjustly deprived of employment and of the remuneration deriving from it, his right to work was violated.
In the Complainant's understanding, the Respondent State violated the provisions of the above-mentioned Articles by not establishing a Constitutional Court and a National Human Rights Institution.

As the procedure indicates, the Respondent State did not respond to the Complainant's observations despite the time limits granted to it for that purpose in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

In its practice, the Commission may render a decision by default where the Respondent State has not submitted its observations at the expiry of the required time limits. On the basis of its jurisprudence and of the findings made in the procedure, the Commission so decides as to the merits of this Communication.

In its precedents, the Commission has held that additional claims are admitted provided that they are based on the same facts, do not call into question matters settled at the admissibility stage, that their author can substantiate them and that the opposing party cannot successfully contest them. The Commission notes that these conditions are met in this case. As to the relevance of the arguments invoked by the Complainant and the default of the Respondent State, the analysis on the merits provides for them. Accordingly, the additional claims and the related requests are received and will be examined.

In its jurisprudence on the right to equal protection of the law, the Commission decided in Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and Another v. Zimbabwe that such a right must be interpreted as the prerogative recognised to every person to have equal access to the courts and to be treated equally by them both in procedure and in substance. According to the Complainant, the fact that the procedure relating to electoral disputes before the Supreme Court does not include a possibility of appeal available before other courts violates his right to equal protection of the law.

The Commission considers that the Complainant's claims relate mainly to the right to equality; that the assessment of whether or not such a right is enjoyed necessarily involves the identification of a comparator in a similar or identical situation, whether real, tacit or assumed. Once the comparator is identified, it must be determined whether the alleged discrimination is justified. Indeed, discrimination is an unlawful or unjustified differentiation, that is, one based on one of the distinctions prohibited in Article 2 of the Charter or any other status.

As to the identification of the comparator, it is for the Commission to determine in the present case, on the one hand, whether the Complainant is in the same situation as ordinary litigants and, on the other, the extent to which the original and final jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in electoral disputes violates the right to equal protection of the law.

On the similarity or identity of situation, the Commission notes that the Complainant was a party to an electoral dispute procedure before the Supreme Court unlike litigants who are parties to proceedings before the ordinary courts. Whereas the procedure before the ordinary courts includes a possibility of appeal and then, possibly, of an appeal on points of law, the Constitution and the electoral law give the Supreme Court jurisdiction to hear electoral disputes at first and last instance. This difference in the organisation of litigation depending on whether constitutional and electoral matters or other matters are involved already places the two categories of litigants in two different situations, which are consequently liable to different treatment based on law.

In principle, such a differentiation cannot constitute discrimination since it is a choice made by the Respondent State to elect the centralised system of litigation rather than the decentralised system. In this regard, the Commission notes that, in general, countries of civil law legal tradition having supreme or constitutional courts of the Kelsenian model adopt the centralised system of constitutional and electoral litigation whereby the competent court hears the dispute at first and last instance. By contrast, in most States of Anglo-Saxon tradition, constitutional litigation is decentralised in that litigants have the possibility of bringing their claims before a lower court and then appealing to a higher court in the event of an unsuccessful application. That said, even in some countries of the second category, electoral disputes may be decentralised as the case may be.

In this case, in order to prove unequal protection of the law, the Complainant should have identified other candidates in the same election who were authorised to bring before the Supreme Court, or another court, an appeal against the judgment rendered by the same Court. By deciding to take part in the legislative election in a constitutional justice system adopting centralised electoral litigation, the Complainant was aware of the choice of system that resulted in a decision rendered at first and last instance. As such, he is ill-founded in alleging a comparison and claiming equal treatment with comparators who are not in a similar or identical situation. Consequently, a violation of the right to equal protection of the law cannot be found, at least as matters stand.

The Complainant alleges the violation of the rights to appeal, to a reasoned decision and to impartial justice. The Commission will examine the arguments invoked in support of each of these allegations.

In support of the allegation of violation of the right to appeal, the Complainant invokes the impossibility of appealing the decisions rendered by the Supreme Court in electoral disputes. As the Commission has previously concluded, the centralised system of electoral litigation falls within the option chosen by the Respondent State. In such a system, constitutional and electoral litigation is entrusted to a single court, placed in most cases at the top of the judicial system. It remains to be seen whether, as the Complainant maintains, such a system violates the right to appeal.

To do so, it is necessary to recall the rationale of the right to appeal before examining the ins and outs of centralised litigation in order to determine to what extent this system does or does not offer the possibility of appeal. On the rationale of the right to appeal, the Commission notes that it pursues three main objectives: 1) to avoid or correct judicial errors and protect the parties against the arbitrariness of the judge; 2) to guarantee legal and judicial certainty through the harmonisation of the law; and 3) to strengthen the legitimacy of the judicial system vis-à-vis the public through the consistent and controlled application of the law that harmonisation provides.

As regards the proponents of the choice of the centralised constitutional or electoral litigation system, the Commission notes that it is often preferred to the decentralised system in that the latter causes the weak rigidity of the Constitution, distrust of the judge, the duality of courts and a split in the legal order. The choice of one or the other of the two systems relates to the legal, historical and socio-political realities of each State. In general, two situations must be distinguished: that in which the highest court enjoying exclusive centralised jurisdiction renders decisions that are not open to any appeal; and that in which the same court renders provisional decisions which may then be subject to appeal in the event of a challenge.

In current practice, the first situation is extremely rare since the supreme courts in charge of electoral litigation almost always render provisional results which may be appealed before the same court. Such a procedure indirectly offers a possibility of contesting the first decision even if only before the same judge. In other cases, the litigation begins before a lower court and then proceeds to appeal or recourse before the highest court. In any event, even in the centralised constitutional or electoral justice system, the final nature of the first decision rendered is only relative since there are almost always remedies such as the application for rectification of a material error and the application for revision of a judgment, among others.

In this case, the Complainant indicates that he was able to submit two applications for rectification of material errors against the decision of the Supreme Court whose regularity he contests. Such a possibility is the manifestation of an option of appeal of the decisions rendered by the Supreme Court. It cannot therefore be considered that the Complainant had no remedy against the first decision rendered. As such, the right to appeal has been respected.

The Commission considers "the guarantee of a decision rendered without undue delay, notified in time and reasoned" as an essential element of the right to a fair hearing in general. It concluded, in Good v. Botswana, that such a right is a component of the right to appeal to competent national organs under Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter. The European and Inter-American Courts of Human Rights have found a violation of the corresponding provisions of their respective conventions to sanction the lack of reasoned decisions.

The requirement for the judge, including the supreme judge, to give reasons for his decisions occupies a central place in fair justice, as attested by both national and international jurisprudence. This position is well illustrated in the decision Dibagula v. The State, in which the Court of Appeal of Tanzania decided that the judge a quo had not respected the right to a fair trial "by simply endorsing the conclusions of the Public Prosecutor without seeking to assess the evidence provided or giving reasons for his decision to adopt the said conclusions. The need for courts to give reasons for their decisions stems from the fact that reasons contribute to clarity and minimise the chances of arbitrariness". The Court of Appeal noted in conclusion that the judge in charge of the case had not only failed to formulate the relevant issues but had not even tried to examine those issues.

As the reasoning must cover both the facts and the law, there is an obligation on the judge to carry out an exhaustive, faithful and fair consideration of the facts of the case. In its judgment in K.K. v. France, the European Court precisely condemns the lack of reasoning on the ground that "whereas the Applicant had presented a fairly detailed account supported by several documents tending to corroborate the facts set out, the trial court dismissed them by means of succinct reasoning".

In the present Communication, the Complainant alleges a lack of reasoning in that, in annulling the initial results that led to his election, the Supreme Court took into account figures that made no reference to the minutes or to other documents authorised by law that would have enabled the Complainant to confirm the effectiveness of the recount. He maintains that the documents that formed the recount, and consequently the Court's decision, were challenged both by the Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI), the institution legally vested with such jurisdiction, and by the witnesses who refused to affix their signatures to the minutes subsequently drawn up. Furthermore, the Court did not, in his view, have the power to invalidate his election but only to order the election to be held again in the constituency concerned.

On these arguments, the Commission notes that, on reading the decisions rendered by the Supreme Court, a distinction must be made according to the allegations made by the Complainant. As regards the reasoning, the Commission notes that judgment RCE.792/DN of 25 April 2012 rendered by the Supreme Court does indeed contain substantial reasoning in that it recalls the facts, the arguments of the parties, develops a line of reasoning and concludes. That said, it must be determined whether, as the Complainant alleges, the Court based its decision on evidence authorised by law, whether the procedure followed was fair and whether it had the legal power to invalidate the Complainant's election and validate that of another candidate in replacement.

As regards the evidence on which judgment RCE.792/DN of 25 April 2012 was based, the Commission notes that under the provisions of Article 56 of the Implementing Measures of Electoral Law No. 11/003 of 25 June 2011, the compilation sheets and minutes are signed by the electoral officials and the witnesses; the minutes and attached documents are transmitted to the Supreme Court by the CENI. In this case, the CENI report of 17 January 2012 produced by the Complainant clearly indicates that the candidates validated by the Supreme Court benefited from fraudulent votes. It follows that if, as noted by the Supreme Court in the said judgment, the documents forming the petition that led to the invalidation of the Complainant's election did not come from the CENI as prescribed by law but rather from the petitioners, there was not a lack of reasoning but rather an absence of legal basis amounting to a lack of grounds.

In connection with the same absence of legal basis, the Commission notes that, under the provisions of Article 75 of Electoral Law No. 006 of 9 March 2006, the Supreme Court has the power to: - confirm the results if they are sincere and regular; - rectify them if they contain material errors; and - annul all or part of them if they are tainted by irregularities having a decisive influence on the outcome of the ballot. If there is no appeal, under the same provisions, a new ballot is organised within sixty (60) days of notification of the decision. Furthermore, it appears that under the provisions of Articles 103(3) and 114(1) of the Constitution, the power to invalidate the election lay with the Plenary of the parliamentary chamber. Finally, the Supreme Court proclaimed seven candidates elected for an electoral constituency where eight were provided for under Article 3 of the Law of 18 August 2011 on the allocation of seats; according to the quotient adopted by the law, the 5,785 votes obtained by the Complainant's party made it eligible for the eighth seat of the constituency.

In this case, in addition to ignoring the quotient adopted by the law and modifying the results by a new count, the Court invalidated the Complainant's election and validated that of another candidate in replacement instead of referring the matter back to the CENI to organise a new ballot. In these circumstances, a violation of the right to a reasoned decision cannot be found either, but rather an absence of legal basis, that is, it must be held that the Court exceeded its powers.

On the other hand, the Commission notes that, in response to the applications for rectification of material error submitted by the Complainant following its decision of invalidation, the Supreme Court responded with decisions one of which was notified late and the other only as to the operative part. The Complainant therefore had no knowledge of the reasons, if any, whereas the said decisions should have explained to the Complainant the responses the judge gave to his claims. As regards these decisions notified only as to the operative part, it must be concluded that the right to a reasoned decision was violated.

As regards the fairness of the procedure, it emerges from the Complainant's arguments that, contrary to the requirements of the electoral law, the Supreme Court carried out a recount of the votes in the absence of the candidates whose election had been invalidated and did not therefore allow them to contest the count and the documents used for it. On these facts, the Commission finds that, rather than the right to a reasoned decision alleged by the Complainant, it is the right to defence, notably that to equality of arms, that was not respected.

In the Commission's consistent jurisprudence, whether or not the time taken in the administration of justice is reasonable is determined mainly in light of the circumstances of the case, the applicable domestic law and the complexity of the issues brought before the courts. In this case, the Commission finds that the court in charge of the dispute was bound by legal time limits to render its decision in petition RCE 792/DN. That said, even if these time limits were exceeded by 18 days, they did not prevent the Complainant from enjoying his right to apply for rectification of material errors. In the specific circumstances of the case, the purpose of the time limits prescribed by law was manifestly to limit the judge in time in order to prevent arbitrariness but above all to enable the petitioner to have the time necessary to prepare a possible appeal within time limits also provided for by law. Consequently, the Commission concludes that there was no violation of the right to be tried within a reasonable time.

As to the lack of impartiality alleged by the Complainant, the Commission notes that impartiality stems mainly from the impression that the judicial system gives to the litigant and thus from a logic related to appearance. The jurisprudence recognises a dual impartiality: objective as to the judge and subjective as to the court. Whereas the former is linked to the personal conviction of the judge, the latter is based on the presumed or actual bias of the court. The burden is on the Complainant to prove the presumption of partiality, which is only rebuttable. In the case examined, the Commission finds that the Complainant proves neither the personal motivation of the judge to take sides, nor the existence of material elements demonstrating the prejudice of the court. The Commission concludes that the violation is not established.

The Complainant alleges the violation of the rights to take part in the conduct of public affairs of his country through the rights to elect and to be elected. These rights fall under Article 13(1) of the Charter. In light of the facts reported and the electoral law of the Respondent State, the Complainant's claims relate to key elements recognised by the relevant international norms as indispensable to the enjoyment of the rights invoked.

The Inter-Parliamentary Union has determined the relevant components of a free and fair electoral process as comprising, among others, the existence of an electoral law and system, a free ballot subject to independent oversight and whose results are published, and a credible mechanism for the management of electoral disputes. These electoral minima are reinforced by the provisions of the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance, which prescribe as necessary conditions for a free and transparent election: to establish and strengthen independent and impartial national electoral bodies responsible for the management of elections; but also to establish and strengthen national mechanisms for the redress of election-related disputes in a timely manner.

In various resolutions on elections in Africa, the Commission emphasises the need for the credibility and independence of the institutions in charge of elections and of the judicial bodies in charge of electoral disputes. In particular, in its Resolution ACHPR/Res.164 (XLVII) 2010 on elections in Africa, the Commission calls on States to ensure that they create conditions conducive to free and transparent elections.

These imperatives are confirmed by the Commission's jurisprudence on the right to political participation. In the case of Constitutional Rights Project and Civil Liberties Organisation v. Nigeria, the Commission concluded that: "The right to freely take part in the government of one's country implies, among other things, the right to vote for the representative of one's choice (...) and that the annulment of the results constitutes a violation of this right". Furthermore, in Lawyers for Human Rights v. Swaziland the Commission decided that "the adoption of a law that prohibits the formation of political parties seriously undermines the ability of citizens to take part in the conduct of the affairs of their country, in violation of Article 13 of the Charter".

These are illustrations of acts of the Respondent State that constitute conduct proscribed by Article 13 in that they have the consequence of preventing the ultimate realisation of the right to political participation. Similar acts therefore fall into the same category. Notably, the minimum that can be required of a Respondent State is to respect the provisions of its own electoral law corresponding to the norms thus set out.

In the present Communication, the Commission notes that the decision of the Supreme Court proceeding to replace the Complainant and consequently to invalidate him as an elected member of Parliament lacked, on the one hand, a legal basis and therefore grounds, and, on the other, reasoning. As the Commission found above, this decision was based on results that could be neither validated by the CENI nor corroborated by the witnesses. Furthermore, the Complainant did not have the opportunity to verify the substance of the recounts that led to the said decision and the judgments were not notified to him in full.

Finally, certain decisions were rendered outside the legal time limits and the Supreme Court proceeded to an invalidation and a replacement even though the electoral law unequivocally prescribed the holding of the election again. These various failings were a breach of the applicable electoral law, notably the provisions of the Constitution and the electoral law of the Respondent State. These breaches of the law necessarily deprived the Complainant, on the one hand, of the votes cast in his favour by the electors and, on the other, of the prerogative to take part in a new election even in the event of a rerun as prescribed by law. The rights protected in Article 13(1) of the Charter have consequently been violated.

The Complainant alleges having been unjustly deprived of employment and the related benefits. In its decisions in Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and Associated Newspapers of Zimbabwe v. Zimbabwe and Pagnoulle (on behalf of Mazou) v. Cameroon, the Commission considered that the right to work covers access to employment, security of employment and reinstatement unless there is appropriate compensation.

The deprivation is manifest in this case. Furthermore, the functions of member of parliament in the National Assembly are conferred by an elective mandate but are for the most part subject to treatment similar to that of the highest-ranking civil servants. The nature of such an activity is permanent, extends over the fixed duration of a mandate and is the subject of remuneration and related benefits. It is therefore an employment the loss of which in the event of non-re-election moreover gives entitlement, in most countries, to unemployment benefit. The Commission has already concluded that the invalidation of the Complainant's election was not in conformity with the law and was consequently unjust. This invalidation prevented him from exercising a remunerated function. The Commission concludes that the provisions of Article 15 have been violated.
In support of the allegations under these provisions, the Complainant invokes the non-existence of a Constitutional Court and of a national human rights institution.

Regarding the obligations incumbent on the State under these provisions, the Commission notes that, as far as judicial institutions are concerned, they must be independent courts and tribunals dispensing justice fairly and impartially as prescribed by the provisions of Article 7 of the Charter. That said, these provisions do not impose on the Respondent State a specific judicial nomenclature, the option for which may depend on imperatives specific to each country. In this case, the fact that the Respondent State vested the Supreme Court with jurisdiction to hear electoral disputes pending the establishment of the Constitutional Court cannot be considered a violation of the aforementioned provisions of the Charter. Indeed, the violation of international human rights conventions could be invoked before the ordinary courts.

As regards the non-existence of institutions specially responsible for the protection and promotion of human rights, the Complainant was able to enjoy the possibility of seizing the Supreme Court of the dispute concerning the election in which he took part. In his specific situation, the Court rendered decisions that are not open to appeal before any other national body, still less a national human rights institution which is not a court. It follows that the Complainant has not been able to prove how the State's failure to establish the Constitutional Court and a national human rights institution violated his rights under Articles 1 and 26 of the Charter.
Since the Commission has accepted some of the Complainant's arguments, the related requests must be examined.

On the request for payment of compensatory damages, the Complainant admits that his reinstatement in the National Assembly is unlikely. The violation of the right to political participation having been established, only compensation equivalent to the loss suffered can redress the harm. While the Complainant puts forward the amount of 25 million United States dollars, he produces neither proof of it nor the scales of calculation. The assessment will therefore be made on the basis of the indices and benefits provided for the calculation of the remuneration of members of the National Assembly.

On the request to require the Respondent State to ratify the Protocol establishing the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights and make the declaration provided for in Article 34(6), the Commission notes that this is a prerogative falling within the discretion and sovereignty of States. The measures to which Article 1 of the Charter obliges States are national and intended to enable the domestic enjoyment of the rights contained in the Charter. Ratification and the declaration are international measures opening access to mechanisms of the same type as the Commission and the Court. As proof, the absence of ratification and declaration did not prevent the Complainant from seizing the Commission after the exhaustion of local remedies. This request should therefore not be granted. Decision of the Commission on the merits The Commission, For these reasons,
Finds that the Democratic Republic of the Congo has not violated the provisions of Articles 3 and 26 of the Charter.

Declares, on the other hand, that the Democratic Republic of the Congo has violated the provisions of Articles 7(1)(a), 13 and 15 of the Charter. Consequently: i. Requests the Democratic Republic of the Congo to pay the Complainant the salaries and benefits due for the period of the mandate during which he was unable to exercise the functions. ii. Further requests the Democratic Republic of the Congo to pay the Complainant damages for the harm suffered as a result of the invalidation. iii. Finally requests the Democratic Republic of the Congo to report to it in writing, within one hundred and eighty (180) days of notification of this decision, on the measures undertaken with a view to implementing these recommendations. Adopted at the 19 Extraordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights held from 16 to 25 February 2016 in Banjul, Islamic Republic of The Gambia.

I am of the opinion, same as all my colleagues, that the Court lacks the jurisdiction to hear and to rule on the "Application" filed by Mr. Femi Falana against the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (hereinafter the "African Commission").

Indeed, according to the Protocol, only States Parties to this instrument may be brought before the Court (see Articles 3 (1), 5 (1, littera c)), 7, 26, 30, 31 and 34 (6)). The African Commission not being a State entity party to the Protocol, the Court manifestly lacks the jurisdiction ratione personae to entertain the said request. Furthermore, by virtue of its subject matter, this request does not fall within the jurisdiction ratione materiae of the Court as envisaged in Article 3 of the Protocol.

Unlike my colleagues, I am however of the view that this request, rather peculiar in nature, cannot in any circumstance be registered in the General List of the Court nor a fortiori, be subject to judicial determination by the Court and be dismissed by way of an Order issued by the Court. It ought to have been rejected by way of a simple letter from the Registrar. *

I shall start by noting that, in his request, Mr. Falana makes no reference to the provisions of the Protocol relating to the Court's jurisdiction in contentious matters (Articles 3 and 5); he merely indicates that "the Application [is brought] pursuant to Rule 29 of the Rules of the African Court which provides that "the Court may also, if it deems it necessary, hear, under rule 45 of the Rules the individual or NGO that initiated a Communication to the Commission pursuant to Article 55 of the Charter"".

This request, which the Registry did not notify to the African Commission nor to other entities listed in Article 35 (3) of the Rules of Court, ought therefore to have been dealt with by way of a simple administrative action, in other words rejected de plano by letter from the Registrar same as in all other cases recently dealt with by the Court in which it manifestly lacked jurisdiction.

It was indeed by office mail signed by the Registrar or Deputy Registrar that "Applications" filed by individuals against non-State entities such as the European Court of Human Rights or the Conférence Interafricaine des Marchés des Assurances (CIMA) were rejected.

In his reply to the author of the latter request, the Registrar thus stated as follows: "[...] I would like to inform you that the Court has no jurisdiction to hear such an appeal for two main reasons: 1) The Court only receives petitions against States (Article 3 of the Protocol). 2) [...]"

In the reply to the request filed against the European Court of Human Rights (and France), the Registrar stated that: “The Registry has decided not to register your Application as it does not meet any of the requirements provided by instruments governing the African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights”. To avoid any ambiguity, the Registrar similarly provided the following clarification: “To be admitted, an Application must, among other conditions, be filed against an African State that is Party to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights and to the Protocol related thereto”.

It is quite rightly that such requests, that the Court manifestly lacks jurisdiction to deal with, were dealt with through an administrative channel. It is moreover consistent with the practice in international jurisdictions such as the International Court of Justice where it is an official of the Registry which is entrusted with replying to requests filed by individuals, entities that do not have a locus standi before the World Court.
It was equally through an administrative channel that the African Court disposed of requests filed by States which are not members of the African Union such as France or Japan.

Thus, in his reply to the request filed against Japan, the Deputy Registrar of the Court stated as follows: “Please be informed that the subject matter of your Application is manifestly not within the jurisdiction of the Court. Further, since your complaint is being made against a non-State Party to the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights on the establishment of an African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights, the Court does not have jurisdiction to receive the matter”.

It was exactly in the same manner that three requests filed against Egypt, a Member State of the African Union but not party to the Protocol, were rejected. In his reply to the latest of these three requests, the Deputy Registrar indeed informed the Applicant as follows: “[...] I would like to inform you that Egypt has not yet ratified the Protocol establishing the Court. The Court can only receive Applications related to States which are Parties to the Protocol”.

It is similarly through an administrative, and not judicial, channel that were rejected Applications filed against States Parties to the Protocol but have not made the optional declaration recognizing as compulsory the Court’s jurisdiction to deal with cases filed by individuals or non-governmental organizations, as provided by Article 34 (6) of the Protocol.

This is for instance the case of an Application filed against Tunisia, in regard to which the Registrar informed the Applicant of what follows: “The Court considered your application and noted that Tunisia, the Respondent against which your Application is filed, has not made the special declaration provided in Article 34 (6) of the Article. It has therefore directed the Registry to inform you that it does not have jurisdiction to deal with your application”. Applications filed against the Republic of Congo and Lesotho were disposed of in the same manner.
I would like to note that none of the abovementioned “matters” was registered in the General List of the Court.

I wish to further note that the judicial determination by the Court of Mr. Falana’s request, filed against an entity which can in any manner whatsoever be brought before the Court, markedly departs from the administrative action decided by the Court, during its 38 Ordinary Session, in the case of Mr. Faustin Uwintije against Rwanda which State is moreover Party to the Protocol and has made the optional declaration recognizing as compulsory the Court’s jurisdiction to deal with cases filed by individuals or non-governmental organizations, as provided by Article 34 (6) of the Protocol. This Application, registered in the General List of the Court, was indeed rejected by way of a simple letter from the Registrar to the Applicant, whereas the Court has manifestly jurisdiction ratione personae to deal with it and has actually considered whether it was well-founded. *

In light of the foregoing, it is my view that the Court ought to have spared itself issuing this Order and thus avoided delving into unnecessary considerations in order to dismiss Mr. Falana's request (paragraphs 8-16). In acting as it did, the Court showed some inconsistency in its reasoning as it had concluded that it lacked the jurisdiction ratione personae to entertain the request (paragraphs 7, 9 and 17), and yet had ruled on it, that is on the "merits" when it concluded that "pursuant to Article 2 of the Protocol and Rule 29 of the Rules, the Court cannot compel the Respondent to seize it". (paragraphs 15 and 18).

This latter conclusion is all the more inopportune as Article 2 of the Protocol and Rule 29 of the Rules to which the Court refers cannot be used as the legal basis for its conclusion that it cannot compel the Commission to refer the matter to it.

Although I do obviously subscribe to this latter conclusion of the Court, I am of the view that the only applicable provision in this case is Article 5 (1) of the Protocol. This provision does indeed allow the Commission to seize the Court; but it does not compel it to do so. This is evident in the French version of paragraph 1 of Article 5, worded as follows: "Ont qualité pour saisir la Cour [...]". The English version of this provision is more straightforward as it states: "The following are entitled to submit cases to the Court [...]" (emphasis added). On the basis of Article 5 (1) littera a) of the Protocol, the Commission is therefore wholly and fully free and independent and cannot in any manner be subject to an injunction from the Court.
Article 29 (3) littera c) of the Rules, which Mr. Falana refers to, can only apply in the circumstance where the Court is properly seized of an Application filed by the African Commission. *

Ultimately, the Court ought not to have dealt with Mr. Falana's request by way of judicial determination. Having opted for that line of action, it ought to have done so in a more straightforward manner and by avoiding to rule on the merits of this request.

I wish to recall as a reminder that this is the fourth time that the African Court has dismissed by way of judicial determination "Applications" filed against non-State entities which by definition cannot be brought before it. The Court having rather limited human and financial resources to deal effectively with a number of cases which is on the increase, it would be advisable not to congest its General List and workload with requests similar to the one considered in the present Order.

We agree substantially with the merits of the judgment of the Court but there is one particular issue on the Order at paragraph 159 which we would approach in a different manner and make a specific order.

The Applicant alleges violation of several articles of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights which have been set out in the judgment and he seeks amongst other reliefs, that he be released from prison.

The Court in its wisdom finds infractions of Articles 1, and 7(1) (a), (c) and (d) of the Charter and Article 14(3)(d) of the ICCPR based largely on lack of fair hearing and then orders the State to:"...take all necessary measures within a reasonable time to remedy the violations found, specifically precluding the reopening of the defence case and the retrial of the Applicant, and to inform the Court, within six (6) months, from the date of this judgment of the measures taken".

On the specific issue as to the Order of his release, the Court opines and we entirely agree that an Order of release of a convict 000983 can only be done in "very specific/and or compelling circumstances". The Court, however goes further to say that the Applicant has not shown exceptional circumstances and this is where we depart.

In spite of the fact that the Application does not state that particular facts exhibit exceptional circumstances, we are of the firm view that the Court found such specific/and or compelling circumstances when it noted that the Applicant has been in prison for 20 years out of the 30 year term of imprisonment and that the reopening of the defence case or a retrial "would result in prejudice and occasion a miscarriage of justice."

We cannot find a more "specific and/or compelling" than that the Applicant has been in prison for about 20 years out of a 30 year prison term following a trial which the Court has declared to be an unfair trial, in violation of the Charter.
Furthermore, there is the recognition that the reopening of the defence or a retrial "would result in prejudice and occasion a miscarriage of justice."
The Court fell shy of making the Order of releasing the Applicant. Our view is therefore that, there is no other remedy in the circumstance other than, that the Applicant be released.

In the circumstance of the case, rather than leaving the issue to the imagination of the Respondent, we would have granted the relief and ordered that the Applicant be released. Done at Arusha this twentieth Day of November 2015 Judge Elsie N.

On 31 December 1996, the Applicant was charged with the offence of armed robbery, allegedly committed along the Kenya/Tanzania border in Rombo District. It was alleged that he stole one hundred (100) sets of clutch covers valued at Tanzania Shillings Eight Hundred Thousand (Tshs. 800,000/=), the property of Mr. Elimani Maleko. He was charged with four other persons before the District Court of Rombo at Mkuu in Criminal Case Number 321 of 1996. The Applicant pleaded not guilty.

On 30 January 1997, the Applicant applied for bail on the grounds of ill health and this application was heard on 31 January 1997 and granted on 5 February 1997. On 20 March 1997 when the matter was mentioned, the Applicant was absent and the Magistrate ordered the arrest of the Applicant and his sureties. On 26 March 1997, when the matter came up for mention and the Court directed the Applicant to show cause why his bail should not be forfeited, he explained that he had been sick. The Court was satisfied with this explanation and, by an order of the same date, extended his bail. The prosecution opened its case on 26 March 1997 and closed its case on 12 June 1997. The Applicant was present throughout the prosecution's case. The defence opened its case on 24 June 1997 and finalised the same on 25 June 1997.

When the defence opened its case on 24 June 1997, the Applicant was absent and the prosecution applied to the trial court that the trial should proceed under Section 226 of the Criminal Procedure Act and that the Applicant be arrested for jumping bail. The application was granted and the matter proceeded under Section 226 of the Criminal Procedure Act. This provision, specifically Section 226(1) thereof, allows the trial court to proceed with a hearing that had been adjourned, if an accused person is not present when the trial resumes. On 25 June 1997, the trial court ordered that a warrant of arrest be issued against the Applicant, and his sureties be summoned to show cause why their bail bond should not be forfeited. The record shows that the Applicant had been admitted to hospital on 20 June 1997, suffering from extra pulmonary tuberculosis and asthmatic statae. He was hospitalised until 21 February 1998.

On 30 June 1997, judgment was delivered in the absence of the Applicant, wherein he was convicted of armed robbery and sentenced to thirty (30) years imprisonment under the Minimum Sentences Act No.1 of 1972 as amended by Miscellaneous Amendment Act No. 10 of 1989. He was also to receive twelve (12) strokes of the cane. The Applicant and the first co-accused were also ordered to pay compensation in respect of the stolen properties yet to be recovered, with a total value of Tanzania Shillings One Hundred and Fifty Thousand (Tshs.150,000/=). The Applicant 001039 commenced his sentence on 3 June 1998 and is currently serving his sentence at Karanga Central Prison at Moshi, Kilimanjaro Region.

The Applicant appealed against his conviction and sentence, vide Criminal Appeal Number 82 of 1998 at the High Court of Tanzania at Moshi. This appeal was dismissed on 23 March 2000. The High Court held that, as the Applicant did not appear when the case was fixed for the defence, he cannot blame the trial court for convicting him in absentia, on the strength of the prosecution's case. The High Court found that the trial magistrate acted properly under section 227 of the Criminal Procedure Act and that the sentence of thirty (30) years' imprisonment is the statutory minimum and therefore dismissed the appeal in its entirety. Section 227 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides as follows: "Where in any case to which section 226 does not apply, an accused being tried by a subordinate court fails to appear on the date fixed for the continuation of the hearing after the close of the prosecution case or on the date fixed for the passing of sentence, the court may, if it is satisfied that the accused's attendance cannot be secured without undue delay or expense, proceed to dispose of the case in accordance with the provisions of section 231 as if the accused, being present, had failed to make any statement or adduce any evidence or, as the case may be, make any further statement or adduce further evidence in relation to any sentence which the court may pass: Provided that - (a) where the accused so fails to appear but his advocate appears, the advocate, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to call any defence witness and to address the court as if the accused had been or is convicted, and the advocate shall be entitled to call any witness and to address the court on matters relevant to any sentence which the court may pass; and (b) where the accused appears on any subsequent date to which the proceedings may have been adjourned, the proceedings under this section on the day or days on which the accused was absent shall not be invalid by reason only of his absence."

Following the dismissal on 23 March 2000, of the Applicant's Appeal to the High Court of Tanzania at Moshi in Criminal Case Number 82 of 1998, the Applicant filed his Notice of Appeal at the Court of Appeal of Tanzania at Moshi on the same date. The Applicant subsequently filed his appeal on 17 April 2003, which was registered as Criminal Appeal Number 153 of 2003.

In order to prosecute this appeal, on 23 April 2003, the Applicant wrote to the High Court requesting for the court record of the proceedings at the High Court in Criminal Case Number 82 of 1998. On 27 January 2004, the Applicant wrote to the Court of Appeal requesting the same, and again on 5 August 2004, to the Registrar of the High Court at Moshi. On 13 September 2004, he wrote a letter to the Registrar of the Court of Appeal requesting a copy of the court record of proceedings at the High Court. On 19 October 2004, the Applicant filed a complaint with the Commission for Human Rights and Good Governance of Tanzania for failure to be furnished with copies of the court record. On 17 June 2005, he wrote a further letter to the Registrar of the Court of Appeal regarding 001037 the delay in having his appeal heard. On 21 September 2005, after the expiry of two (2) years and five (5) months, the Applicant's appeal to the Court of Appeal, Criminal Appeal Number 153 of 2003, was heard and dismissed. At the time of the hearing of this appeal, the Applicant had not been provided with a copy of the court record. The Appeal was dismissed for being filed out of time.

On 31 October 2005, the Applicant made an application to the High Court at Moshi, vide Miscellaneous Criminal Application Number 40 of 2005, for leave to file his Notice of Appeal out of time. The High Court of Tanzania at Moshi granted his Application, on 12 February 2007 and on the same date, the Applicant filed a Notice of Appeal to the Court of Appeal, being Criminal Appeal Number 217 of 2007. On 28 June 2007, and after the expiry of four (4) years and six (6) months, the Applicant received the record of proceedings in Criminal Appeal Number 82 of 1998 at the High Court of Tanzania at Moshi. On 15 October 2007, Criminal Appeal Number 217 of 2007 was struck out on the basis that the Notice of Appeal was unsigned and was filed out of time.

On 7 February 2008, the Applicant filed Miscellaneous Criminal Case Number 3 of 2007 at the High Court of Tanzania at Moshi seeking that his Notice of Appeal be heard out of time. In the course of the proceedings for this application, the Applicant requested to amend the application in order to cite the proper provisions applicable and the Court granted this application. The Court ordered that the Applicant file the amended application before 11 June 2008. In compliance with this order, on 6 June 2008, the Applicant applied to the High Court of Tanzania at Moshi vide 001036 Amended Miscellaneous Application Number 3 of 2008, seeking leave to lodge a fresh appeal out of time. On 11 June 2008, the High Court, being satisfied that the Applicant had complied with the Order to file the amended Application, granted the Applicant leave to file the Notice of Appeal to the Court of Appeal within ten (10) days thereof. On 13 June 2008, the Applicant filed at the High Court of Tanzania at Moshi, a Notice of Appeal to the Court of Appeal. This new appeal to the Court of Appeal was filed as Criminal Appeal Number 230 of 2008.

On 10 July 2008, the Applicant wrote a letter to the Registrar of the Court of Appeal to inform him of the delay in the hearing of his appeal. On 2 February 2009 the Applicant wrote a letter to the District Registrar of the High Court of Tanzania at Moshi requesting the record of the proceedings at the High Court. On 17 March 2009, the Applicant received a copy of the court record.

On 29 May 2009, the Court of Appeal delivered its judgment in Criminal Appeal Number 230 of 2008, dismissing the appeal, and finding that the prosecution's case had merit, upheld the Applicant's conviction and sentence.

On 10 June 2009, the Applicant filed a Notice of Motion for review of the decision of the Court of Appeal in Criminal Appeal Number 230 of 2008. On 4 January 2010, the Applicant wrote to the Chief Justice of the United Republic of Tanzania reminding him of his request for pro bono legal counsel and requesting hearing of his Application for Review.

Though it is not clear from the record when the Applicant first requested for pro bono legal counsel, on 3 September 2010, the Applicant wrote a further letter reminding the Chief Justice of his request for pro bono legal counsel and requesting hearing of his Application for Review.

The Applicant alleges that, at the time of filing this Application at the African Court on 2 August 2013, he has received "no substantive response as to the status of his review".
The Respondent raises preliminary objections on issues of jurisdiction and admissibility.

The Respondent contends that the Applicant's citation of Articles 5 and 34(6) of the Protocol and Rule 33 of the Rules of Court to invoke the jurisdiction of the Court is not proper as these articles only provide him standing before the Court. The Respondent argues that, therefore, the jurisdiction of the Court has not been invoked.

The Respondent contends further that, the Application does not refer to, or ask for, the interpretation or application of the Charter, the Protocol or any other relevant human rights instrument ratified by the United Republic of Tanzania. The Applicant has merely listed his grievances against the application of the Criminal Procedure Act in relation to the originating criminal case against him, being Case Number 321 of 1996.
The Respondent asserts that, because the Applicant is not clear in the remedies he seeks, he therefore, has not invoked the jurisdiction of the Court and the Application should be dismissed.

The Applicant maintains that the Court has the jurisdiction ratione materiae to determine this case on the basis that there are allegations of violations of the human rights of the Applicant as guaranteed under the Charter.

In the Reply to the Respondent's Response, the Applicant alleges violation of the obligation of Member States to give effect to the rights, duties and freedoms enshrined therein, violation of the right to equality before the law and equal protection of the law and violation of the prohibition of torture, cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment which resulted from the inordinate delay in the hearing of the Applicant's cases. The Applicant also states that his right to personal liberty and protection from arbitrary arrest have been violated by his continued detention occasioned by the delay in the hearing of his cases. He asserts that his right to a fair trial was violated because he was not given the opportunity to present his defence, he was not provided pro bono legal aid despite being charged with a serious offence and that there were systematic and prolonged delays in his appeals and his application for review at the Court of Appeal. The Applicant maintains that these delays were compounded by the dilatory conduct of the state in providing the record of proceedings of the trial courts which hampered his ability to file his appeal. The Applicant maintains that this also violated his right to receive information and his right to freedom of expression.

The Applicant also argues that, the Court has jurisdiction ratione personae and that he is entitled to file an Application before the Court on the basis that he is a citizen of the United Republic of Tanzania, and the Respondent State has ratified the Protocol and filed a declaration allowing direct access for individuals to file cases before this Court.

The Applicant further asserts that, the Court has held a similar view on its jurisdictional requirements in Application Number 001/2012 Frank David Omary and Others v The United Republic of Tanzania and Application Number 003/2012 Peter Joseph Chacha v The United Republic of Tanzania.

The Court considers that the Respondent's objection that "the Court lacks jurisdiction because the Applicant improperly cites Articles 5 and 34(6) of the Protocol and Rule 33 of the Rules of Court and that the Articles only provide him standing before the Court" lacks merit. The Court finds that as long as the rights allegedly violated are protected by the Charter or any other human rights instrument ratified by the State concerned, the Court will have jurisdiction over the matter. The Court first elaborated on this in Application Number 001/2012 Frank David Omary and Others v United Republic of Tanzania and thereafter, in Application Number 003/2012 Peter Joseph Chacha v United Republic of Tanzania. The Court, in the above cases held that, the substance of the complaint must relate to rights guaranteed by the Charter or any other human rights instrument ratified by the State concerned. It is not necessary that the rights alleged to have been violated are specified in the Application.
In any event, in the instant case, the Applicant's Reply to the Respondent's Response specifies the rights guaranteed by the Charter alleged to have been violated (supra paragraph 42).
The Court finds that the Applicant's Application states facts which relate to human and peoples' rights protected under the Charter, and therefore holds that it has jurisdiction ratione materiae.

Although the parties raised an issue purportedly relating to the Court's jurisdiction ratione personae, the Court does not consider this to be an objection on its jurisdiction ratione personae. The Respondent is a State Party to the Protocol, which has also made the declaration in terms of Article 34(6) of the Protocol accepting the seizure of the Court by an individual. The Respondent deposited its instrument of ratification of the Protocol on 10 February 2006 and deposited the declaration required under 34(6) of the Protocol on 29 March 2010. Though the alleged violations occurred before the deposit of the instruments of ratification and declaration aforementioned, the Court finds that it has jurisdiction ratione personae.

The Respondent raises preliminary objections on admissibility based on different components of the requirements of Article 56 of the Charter. These are on incompatibility of the Application with the Charter and the Constitutive Act of the African Union, on non-exhaustion of local remedies and in the alternative thereto, that the Application has not been filed within a reasonable time from when local remedies were exhausted.

The Respondent contends that the Application does not comply with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the Charter as it does not address issues compatible with the Charter or the principles enshrined in the Charter of the Organisation of African Unity and further, that no provisions of the African Charter have been referenced in the Application.

The Applicant avers that he has met the requirements of Article 56(2) of the Charter which stipulate that applications must be compatible thereto. This is because, the Court has decided, in Application Number 003/2012 Peter Joseph Chacha v The United Republic of Tanzania that, so long as the rights alleged to have been violated are contained in the Charter, they need not be specifically cited in the application.

Regarding the Respondent's objection to the application on the grounds of its incompatibility with the Charter of the Organization of African Unity, now the Constitutive Act of the African Union, the Court notes that this argument lacks merit. The Constitutive Act of the African Union provides that one of the objectives of the African Union shall be to promote and protect human and peoples' rights in accordance with the Charter and other relevant human rights instruments. In addition, the Court finds that the Applicant's Application states facts which relate to human and peoples' rights protected under the Charter. Moreover, the Court has decided on this issue in Application Number 001/2012 Frank David Omary and Others v United Republic of Tanzania and Application Number 003/2012 Peter Joseph Chacha v United Republic of Tanzania. In the latter case, the Court found that "... the Applicant's Application states facts which revealed a prima facie violation of his rights; furthermore, the Court finds that the Application relates to human and peoples' rights protected under the Charter, therefore the requirements of Article 3(1) of the Protocol and Article 56(2) of the Charter have been met".

The Respondent states that the application has not been filed after exhausting local remedies. The Respondent states that the N.G. Applicant should have waited for the 5 June 2009 Notice of Motion to Review the Court of Appeal's decision in Criminal Appeal Number 230 of 2008 to be heard. The Respondent further states that the Applicant could have also instituted a Constitutional Petition before the High Court of Tanzania vide the Basic Rights and Duties Enforcement Act, 1994, regarding the alleged violation of his rights, which form the basis of his application before this Court.
The Applicant avers that local remedies were fully exhausted when the Court of Appeal of Tanzania, the highest court of the land, finally and in its entirety, dismissed his appeal on 29 May 2009.

The Applicant avers that one need not file an application for review so as to exhaust local remedies. He also states that the assertion of the Respondent State that the Applicant should have filed a constitutional petition to challenge the delay in the hearing of the review is both unnecessary and redundant as it imposes a requirement to utilise a procedure that falls outside the scope of the rule requiring exhaustion of local remedies.

On the preliminary objection that the Applicant did not exhaust local remedies, the Court finds that the Applicant went through the required criminal trial process up to the highest Court in the land and finally applied for review to the Court of Appeal. In a case involving the Respondent State before the African Commission, the Respondent State maintained that the Court of Appeal is the highest Court in the land. Additionally, the procedures followed on local remedies were unduly prolonged.

The Court finds that there were systematic and prolonged delays in the determination of his appeal to the Court of Appeal. Following the dismissal, on 23 March 2000 of the Applicant's appeal to the High Court, being Criminal Appeal Number 82 of 1998, it was only on 17 April 2003 that his Appeal to the Court of Appeal was registered. There were also unreasonable delays in providing the Applicant with the record of proceedings of the appeal heard by the High Court, (Criminal Appeal Number 82 of 1998), which he required to prosecute his Appeal at the Court of Appeal. A period of two (2) years and five (5) months lapsed between 23 April 2003, when the Applicant first requested for this record of proceedings, and 21 September 2005, when the appeal at the Court of Appeal was heard and dismissed, for being filed out of time. The Court notes that by the time the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal, the Applicant was yet to be provided with the record of the proceedings of Criminal Appeal Number 82 of 1998.

The Applicant then filed a Miscellaneous Application at the High Court, on 31 October 2005, seeking leave to file his Notice of Appeal to the Court of Appeal, out of time. Once this application was granted on 12 February 2007, his new appeal to the Court of Appeal was registered on the same date, as Criminal Appeal Number 217 of 2007. It was only after the filing of this second appeal to the Court of Appeal that, on 28 June 2007, four (4) years and six (6) months after first requesting for the record of proceedings of the appeal at the High Court (Criminal Appeal Number 82 of 1998), the Applicant received the record. However, on 15 October 2007, the Court of Appeal struck out Criminal Appeal Number 217 of 2007 on the basis that the Notice of Appeal was unsigned and was filed out of time.

On 7 February 2008, the Applicant filed a Miscellaneous Application at the High Court seeking leave to file his Appeal out of time. This application was subsequently granted and on 13 June 2008, the Applicant filed a new appeal to the Court of Appeal vide Criminal Appeal Number 230 of 2008. This appeal was dismissed on 29 May 2009 on the basis that the prosecution had proven the case against the Applicant in the original criminal case. The Applicant represented himself throughout these processes, despite the fact that the charges against him were serious offences and carried a heavy custodial sentence and his requests for pro bono legal counsel were not responded to.

Regarding the Respondent's contention that the Applicant should have applied for a constitutional petition to vindicate his rights under the Basic Rights and Duties Enforcement Act, the Court finds that the Applicant was not under an obligation to do so. The alleged non-conformity by the trial court, with the due process, with its bundle of rights and guarantees, formed the basis of his appeals to the High Court and the Court of Appeal. The Court of Appeal decided on the Applicant's appeal with finality therefore he accessed the highest Court in the Respondent State.

Furthermore, the Court notes that if in proceedings in a subordinate court, basic rights are alleged to have been contravened, an application is made under the Basic Rights and Duties Enforcement Act, to the High Court to be decided by a three – Judge Bench and an appeal therefrom lies to the Court of Appeal.

In the instant case, once the Court of Appeal of Tanzania decided on the Applicant's appeal, it would have been unreasonable to require him to lodge a fresh application regarding his right to a fair trial, to the High Court, which is a court lower than the Court of Appeal of Tanzania.

Regarding the Respondent's contention that the Applicant should have pursued the application for review to its conclusion, the Court finds that this was neither necessary nor mandatory. The final appeal in criminal trials lies, as of right, to the Court of Appeal, which the Applicant has proved that he accessed.
